decisions.title: Shell auto-activation for jet env
decisions.gist: Whether entering a project directory activates its env automatically or stays explicit.
decisions.lesson:
An env in Jet is a per-project dev shell, declared in env.jet, that sets tools and variables for that project.

A shell hook is a small snippet the shell runs on every directory change, so a tool can react to where you are.

direnv is the popular tool that pioneered this: cd into a project and its environment loads, leave and it unloads.

A trust prompt is Jet's ratified rule that the first time an untrusted directory would run code, the tool asks the user to approve it.

Opt-in means nothing happens until the user installs the hook themselves with one line.
decisions.story:
Warren Boyd hops between six repos a day. Each needs its own toolchain and variables.

With explicit activation he types jet env enter in every one, and forgets it often enough to debug with the wrong tool version. His direnv habit trained him to expect the shell to just follow the project.

He wants cd into a repo to load its env, and cd out to drop it, safely.
decisions.inWild: A developer clones a repo containing env.jet and changes into it. They expect the right compiler and environment variables to be active with no manual command, but only after approving an unfamiliar project once.

options.name: Opt-in cd-activation hook
options.detail:
jet env hook <shell> prints a hook the user adds to their shell config once. After that, entering a directory with env.jet activates it, and leaving deactivates.

The first activation of an untrusted env uses the same trust prompt as the rest of Jet. JET_ENV_DISABLE turns it off anywhere.
options.code:
# install once:
$ jet env hook fish | source   # or add to config.fish

$ cd ~/work/router
jet: env.jet in this directory is not yet trusted. Activate it? [y/N] y
jet env: activated (jet 0.9, PGHOST=localhost)

$ cd ..
jet env: deactivated

$ JET_ENV_DISABLE=1 cd ~/work/router   # no activation this session

options.name: Status quo: explicit enter only
options.detail:
Keep activation manual. The user runs jet env or jetpack enter in each project.

Nothing runs on cd, so there is no hook to install, but the developer must remember every time.
options.code:
$ cd ~/work/router
$ jet env enter        // must remember, every directory, every session
jet env: activated

# forget it and you build with the wrong toolchain, no warning

comparisons.note: direnv made cd-activation the habit a generation of developers now expect, guarded by an explicit allow per directory. Jet mirrors the model and reuses its own trust prompt for the approval step.
comparisons.code:
$ cd myproject
direnv: error .envrc is blocked. Run `direnv allow` to approve.

comparisons.note: mise activate installs a shell hook that swaps toolchains per directory. It proved the one-line opt-in install is the right ergonomic. Jet follows the same shape with jet env hook.
comparisons.code: eval "$(mise activate zsh)"   # one line in your shell config

recommendation.why:
Auto-activation is the ergonomic developers already expect from direnv and mise, and forgetting to activate is a real source of wrong-toolchain bugs. The hook removes that whole failure mode.

It stays safe because the first activation of an unfamiliar project goes through Jet's existing trust prompt.
recommendation.tradeoff: A shell hook runs on every directory change, so it must stay fast and is opt-in rather than on by default. The payoff is that the environment always matches the project you are in.

whyNot.reason: Explicit enter is easy to forget, which silently builds with the wrong toolchain and gives no warning. It leaves a papercut every other tool in this space has already removed.

hybrid.synthesis: The opt-in hook is the feature, and the explicit enter of option B stays available for one-off shells and for anyone who declines to install the hook. Auto by choice, manual always possible.

harvest.use: Ship as jet env hook, opt-in, reusing the ratified trust and disable controls.
Keep as the manual path for scripts, one-off shells, and users who prefer no hook.

decisions.title: Live runtime inspector
decisions.gist: Whether Jet gets a live view of a running program or relies on post-mortem traces.
decisions.lesson:
A task is Jet's unit of concurrent work, and tasks form a tree as one spawns another.

A channel is a typed pipe between tasks. Its depth is how many messages are waiting, and a full channel means a producer is blocked.

A deadline is a time budget on a task, from the ratified #Context machinery.

An arena is a region of memory freed all at once. Its stats show how much the program is holding.

Post-mortem means you inspect a recording after the run. Live means you attach to a process and watch it right now. .jtrace and jet perf are Jet's existing recording and profiling rails.
decisions.story:
Clara Dawson's data pipeline hangs in staging. Nothing crashes; it just stops making progress.

A post-mortem trace tells her what happened after she kills it, but not what is stuck while it hangs. She needs to see, right now, which channel is full and which task is blocked on it.

In Erlang she would open observer and watch the process live. Jet's runtime is opaque while it runs.
decisions.inWild: A running pipeline stalls with no error. The developer wants a live picture of the task tree, each channel's depth, pending deadlines, and current effect activity, without stopping the process.

options.name: jet inspect live
options.detail:
jet inspect live shows a live task tree, channel depths, deadlines, effect activity, and arena stats. It attaches to a jet dev session or any process started with observe enabled.

It is a viewer over the existing observability rails, not a new fact producer. The same facts feed Canvas's proof rail.
options.code:
$ jet inspect live --attach 48213
task tree                         chan depth    deadline
main                                            -
 ingest         running          in:0          -
   transform    BLOCKED          out:1024/1024 480ms
     write      idle             -             -
effects: Db.Read x3   Net.Send x0
# transform is blocked pushing to a full channel; write task is idle

options.name: Post-mortem only
options.detail:
No live attach. Richer .jtrace recording plus the jet perf viewer cover analysis after the run.

Good for a run that finishes or crashes. Useless for a hang you must observe while it is happening.
options.code:
$ jet run --trace pipeline.jet     // records a .jtrace
$ jet perf view pipeline.jtrace    // inspect afterward

// but a live hang never ends, so there is no finished trace:
$ jet perf view pipeline.jtrace
error: trace is incomplete; process still running

comparisons.note: observer shows every process, mailbox, and memory cell of a live node, and is the tool Erlang developers reach for on a stuck system. jet inspect live brings that live picture to Jet's tasks and channels.
comparisons.code: 1> observer:start().   %% live process and mailbox view

comparisons.note: Go has pprof for profiling and a goroutine dump on demand, but no continuous live view of a running scheduler. A dedicated live inspector fills that exact gap.
comparisons.code: curl localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2   # a one-shot dump, not live

recommendation.why:
A hang has no post-mortem, because the run never ends, so only a live view can show which channel is full and which task is blocked. That is the case where developers are most stuck.

It adds no new fact producer. It views the observability rails that already exist and feeds the same facts to Canvas.
recommendation.tradeoff: Live attach means a process must expose an inspection endpoint, on by default in jet dev and opt-in elsewhere. The benefit is diagnosing a stall while it is happening rather than guessing after.

whyNot.reason: Post-mortem traces cannot help with a hang that never terminates, which is the motivating failure. Profiling a finished run is a different job the perf viewer already covers.

hybrid.synthesis: The live inspector and the post-mortem tools are complementary views over the same observability facts. jet inspect live handles the running system, and .jtrace and jet perf handle the finished one.

harvest.use: Ship as jet inspect live for stalls and running-system diagnosis, feeding Canvas's proof rail.
Keep .jtrace and jet perf as the post-mortem path for completed or crashed runs.

decisions.title: Windows COM automation binder (the Office / VBA estate)
decisions.gist: How Jet reaches the Windows COM estate — Excel, Word, and Outlook automation plus VBA-macro migration.
decisions.lesson:
COM is the Windows component ABI. It is a binary contract that lets one program drive another. Office exposes all of its features through COM.

IDispatch is COM's dynamic call interface. A caller invokes methods by name at runtime instead of through a fixed table.

A type library is a machine-readable description of a component's API. It names the methods, arguments, and types.

VBA is the macro language that scripts Office through COM. Millions of business workbooks carry VBA logic that nobody wants to lose.
decisions.story:
Ruth Callahan runs the quarterly close for a finance team. Their reporting lives in twenty Excel workbooks driven by VBA macros.

The macros are fragile and the person who wrote them left years ago. Ruth wants to automate the close from a Jet service today.

She also wants to migrate the macros into Jet gradually, without a big-bang rewrite that could change a number.
decisions.inWild:
use com.excel as xl

wb :: xl.workbooks.open("q3.xlsx")?
wb.sheet("Summary").cell("B4").set(total)
wb.save()?

options.name: com.* root, Windows-gated, typed stubs from the type library
options.detail: Mount COM as `com.*`, Windows-only with an honest gated error elsewhere (the ratified swift precedent). `use com.excel as xl` binds from the installed type library. `jet inspect bind com` generates committable typed stubs, the way the js binder emits `.d.ts` stubs. Libraries with no type library get a dynamic IDispatch fallback behind `#Unsafe`. The same surface serves both live automation and VBA-estate migration, since the D-MIGRATE-SRC1 importer emits Jet calling `com.*`.
options.code:
use com.excel as xl                       // binds from the installed type library

fn write_summary(total: Money) -> Unit ? ComError {
    wb :: xl.workbooks.open("q3.xlsx")?
    wb.sheet("Summary").cell("B4").set(total)
    wb.save()?
}

// On a non-Windows host the gated error is honest, like swift off macOS:
$ jet build --target linux
error[E3260]: `com.*` needs a Windows host
  ── close.jet:1:5
  use com.excel as xl
      ^^^^^^^^^ COM automation runs only on Windows
  = help: build with --target windows, or run this module on a Windows host

options.name: No COM root — pwsh sidecar or hand C FFI
options.detail: Ship no `com.*` root. Office automation goes through a pwsh sidecar or a hand-written C FFI layer over raw IDispatch. Both work, both are miserable, and both concede the estate. Values cross as interpolated text with no type checks, and there is no migration path.

comparisons.note: pywin32 drives Office through late-bound IDispatch. Calls are dynamic, so a misspelled property or a wrong type fails at runtime, not before. Jet's typed stubs from the type library move those failures to build time.
The old estate glue is VBScript over COM, now deprecated on modern Windows. It has no types and no package story. A typed com.* surface replaces it without a rewrite of the underlying components.

recommendation.why: Option A is the only path that both automates the estate and migrates it. The type library gives a typed, checked surface with no string scraping. The gated error follows the ratified swift precedent, so non-Windows builds fail clearly. The IDispatch fallback still reaches old components that ship no type library.
recommendation.tradeoff: The `com.*` surface runs only on Windows. That is inherent to COM, not a Jet limit. A cross-platform caller wraps the module behind a service boundary and calls it from a Windows host.

whyNot.reason: Option B leaves Office behind a stringly-typed pwsh script or a hand-marshaled C shim. Values cross as interpolated text, so a wrong cell type fails at runtime instead of at build. It also gives no migration path, so the VBA estate stays trapped.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship A. The typed type-library surface is the default. IDispatch behind `#Unsafe` is the escape hatch for components with no type library. The pwsh path from B stays available for one-off glue, never as the Office story.

harvest.use: the shipped com.* surface with committable stubs
pwsh sidecar remains for throwaway automation outside the estate

decisions.title: PowerShell binder and object pipeline
decisions.gist: How Jet calls PowerShell and carries its object pipeline across the boundary.
decisions.lesson:
PowerShell is Microsoft's automation shell and scripting language. PowerShell 7 runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

A cmdlet is a built-in command that returns objects, not text. PowerShell pipelines pass whole objects between commands rather than strings.

DataTree is Jet's ratified dynamic value. It is a self-describing tree of typed fields, and it is how loosely shaped foreign data crosses into Jet.
decisions.story:
Frank Delgado runs a Windows operations team. Years of runbooks manage Active Directory and Exchange through PowerShell cmdlets.

A new Jet service needs to call those runbooks and read their results. Frank does not want to rewrite them or scrape their console text, which reformats between versions.

options.name: Sidecar pwsh worker, objects cross as DataTree
options.detail: Run a supervised sidecar pwsh 7 worker, matching the ratified Python model. Cmdlet results cross as `DataTree`, since PowerShell objects are property bags. Whole pipelines are callable as Jet functions, and field access is checked at the boundary. The effect root is `#(Pwsh)`.

options.name: Shell-out only via Sh typed text
options.detail: Reach PowerShell only by launching `pwsh -c` through the ratified `Sh` typed text. This loses the object pipeline entirely. Results come back as formatted console text that the caller must scrape column by column, with no types.
options.code:
use core.process

cmd: Sh :: "pwsh -c \"Get-Mailbox | Format-Table Name,LastLogon\""
out :: process.run(cmd)?

// out.stdout is raw text — parse the columns yourself, no types:
rows :: out.stdout.lines().map(l -> l.split_whitespace())

comparisons.note: Bash pipes bytes between commands, so every stage re-parses text. PowerShell pipes objects, so fields keep their types. Option A preserves that. Scraping the text throws it away.
comparisons.code: ps aux | grep bash | awk '{print $2}'   # re-parse at every stage

recommendation.why: Option A keeps PowerShell's whole point, which is objects rather than text. Cmdlet results cross as DataTree with typed field access checked at the boundary. The sidecar runs cross-platform pwsh 7, so a Linux Jet service can drive Windows runbooks over a remote session.
recommendation.tradeoff: The sidecar adds a worker process and a typed message hop. That isolation is the same crash-safe model already ratified for Python and Ruby.

whyNot.reason: Option B shells out and scrapes formatted text. It discards the object pipeline, so every result is untyped string columns. A renamed column silently breaks the parsing with no diagnostic at all.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship A. The object-preserving sidecar is the default. The `Sh` path from B still exists through the ratified D-FFI-SH1 surface for a bare one-line invocation. Any structured work uses the DataTree surface.

harvest.use: the shipped pwsh sidecar and DataTree rows
D-FFI-SH1 Sh text covers a one-off pwsh -c with no result parsing

decisions.title: Dart binder and Flutter embedding direction
decisions.gist: How Jet interoperates with Dart, and whether it also embeds into Flutter apps.
decisions.lesson:
Dart is Google's application language. Flutter is Google's UI toolkit, written in Dart, for mobile, web, and desktop apps.

dart_api_dl is Dart's C interop layer. It lets native code call into a running Dart runtime.

A C ABI is the plain C calling convention that every language can link against. A c-archive is a static library exposing C-ABI entry points.

Flutter apps reach native code through platform channels or through C FFI.
decisions.story:
Grace Holloway leads a small product team. They ship a Flutter mobile app and a backend service.

Both need the same pricing-and-rules engine. Today the logic is copied into Dart and into the server, and the two copies drift apart.

Grace wants one Jet core called from both sides, so a rule change lands in exactly one place.

options.name: Dual surface — dart.* binder plus Flutter C-ABI embedding
options.detail: Bind Dart libraries through `dart.*` over dart_api_dl. Also ship the embedding path: a Jet library compiled to a C-ABI archive through the existing plugin and c-archive machinery, callable from a Flutter app. Embedding is the direction mobile teams reach for first.

options.name: dart.* library binder only, no embedding
options.detail: Ship only the `dart.*` library binder over dart_api_dl. Jet can call Dart packages, but nothing lets a Flutter app call a Jet core. The app keeps its own copy of the shared logic.

options.name: Defer until the native mobile UI decision (#480)
options.detail: Ship no `dart` root yet. Wait until E3-UL9 / card #480 decides Jet's native mobile UI strategy, then design the Dart story around that outcome.
options.code:
$ jet build --target plugin
error[E3299]: no `dart` binder — deferred pending the mobile UI decision (#480)
  = help: no interop path to a Flutter app is available yet

comparisons.note: Flutter's own native bridge serializes messages across an async channel, so calls are stringly-keyed and asynchronous. A C-ABI archive links directly, so the shared engine is a plain typed function call with no message hop.
comparisons.code: await channel.invokeMethod('quote', {'qty': qty});  // async, untyped map

recommendation.why: Option A ships the direction mobile teams reach for first, which is one Jet engine linked into the Flutter app as a C-ABI archive. It also binds Dart libraries through dart_api_dl. This binder is the interop floor no matter how #480 rules on native mobile UI.
recommendation.tradeoff: The embedding side reuses the existing plugin and c-archive machinery, so the app links a static library and a header. The library side needs a running Dart runtime, provisioned by jetpack.

whyNot.reason: Option B binds Dart libraries but gives no embedding path. Grace's real need, one engine shared with the Flutter app, stays unmet, and the two copies keep drifting.
Option C defers everything and blocks Grace today. The C-ABI interop floor is useful whatever #480 decides about native UI, so waiting buys nothing.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship A. The C-ABI embedding path is the headline. The `dart.*` library binder rides the same ballot. Whatever #480 later decides about native mobile UI builds on top of this interop floor, never around it.

harvest.use: C-ABI embedding and the dart.* binder both ship
the dart.* binder half is exactly B, kept inside A
the #480 dependency is noted honestly, not used to block the interop floor

decisions.title: Tcl binder host model (the EDA tooling estate)
decisions.gist: Whether Jet embeds Tcl in-process or runs it as a sidecar, for the chip-design tool estate.
decisions.lesson:
Tcl is a small scripting language built from the start to be embedded inside other programs.

EDA means electronic design automation. It is the software that turns chip and FPGA designs into real hardware. Vivado, Quartus, and Synopsys drive their flows through Tcl scripts.

Place-and-route is the step that positions logic on a chip and wires it together. These flows emit their results as Tcl values.
decisions.story:
Wes Harmon builds FPGA images for a hardware team. The vendor toolchain is driven entirely by Tcl scripts.

Wes wants a Jet pipeline to launch a place-and-route run and read its timing results. Today he shells out and greps the log, which breaks whenever the tool reformats its output.
decisions.inWild:
use tcl.vivado as vivado

session :: vivado.open("top.xpr")?
timing :: session.report_timing()?
assert(timing.worst_slack >= 0.0, "setup timing violated")

options.name: In-process interpreter with live sessions
options.detail: Embed a Tcl interpreter in-process, the way Tcl was designed to run and the way every EDA tool already hosts it. A design session stays live across calls, so place, route, and timing steps share state. Tcl dicts cross as typed fields. Long runs declare a `#(Tcl)` effect.

options.name: Sidecar tclsh worker
options.detail: Run Tcl as a separate `tclsh` process and evaluate strings against it. Interpreter state does not persist between calls without a hand-rolled session protocol, so a multi-step flow keeps re-sourcing scripts. Results still come back as text to scrape.

comparisons.note: The vendor tools host a Tcl interpreter inside their own process and expose their whole API as Tcl commands. An in-process Jet interpreter matches that model, so sessions and design state stay live between calls.
comparisons.code: vivado -mode tcl -source build.tcl   # the tool itself IS a Tcl host

recommendation.why: Option A embeds Tcl in-process, the way Tcl was designed and the way every EDA tool already hosts it. A design session stays live across calls, so place, route, and timing share state. Results cross as typed values, so a slack check is a real assertion rather than a log grep.
recommendation.tradeoff: The in-process interpreter shares the host process, matching the ratified Lua model. A long tool run still declares a `#(Tcl)` effect, so blocking stays visible.

whyNot.reason: Option B runs a separate tclsh and evaluates strings. Interpreter state does not persist between calls without a hand-rolled protocol, so a multi-step flow keeps re-sourcing scripts. Results still come back as text to scrape.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship A. The in-process interpreter with live sessions is the default and matches how the EDA tools themselves run. The plain `tcl.eval` one-shot from B is available for a stateless script, but the session surface is the estate's real entry.

harvest.use: the shipped in-process interpreter with typed results
tcl.eval covers a single self-contained script with no session

decisions.title: Ada binder with constraint facts (the certified-code estate)
decisions.gist: How Jet reuses certified Ada libraries while keeping their range checks at the boundary.
decisions.lesson:
Ada is a systems language used where failure is unacceptable — avionics, rail, and defense.

GNAT is the open-source Ada compiler in the GCC family. Ada can mark a routine as C-callable with pragma Export and pragma Convention.

Ada types carry ranges and constraints, so a value outside its declared range is an error the language enforces.

jet prove is Jet's static-proof mode. It matches the assurance culture around Ada and its SPARK subset.
decisions.story:
Ellen Marsh is an engineer at an avionics supplier. Her group owns a certified Ada library for geodesy, the math that turns sensor angles into ground positions.

New ground-station software is being written in Jet. Ellen must reuse the certified library exactly, without re-certifying a rewrite, and keep its range checks intact.
decisions.inWild:
use ada.geodesy as geo

pos :: geo.to_ecef(lat: 47.6, lon: -122.3, alt_m: 130.0)?

options.name: GNAT C-ABI binder that transports constraint facts
options.detail: Bind Ada through its C-ABI exports (pragma Export, Convention C), following the ratified Fortran model. The binder drives gnatmake and reads the Ada spec. It records each range and constraint into the binding, so an out-of-range Jet value is a checked error before the call. This pairs with `jet prove`.

options.name: No root — hand-written C shims
options.detail: Ship no `ada.*` root. Reach the library through hand-written C shims declared in an `#Extern` overlay under `#Unsafe`. Every Ada range constraint is dropped, so a bad value faults inside the Ada runtime at run time.

comparisons.note: GNAT already emits C-callable entry points with pragma Export and Convention C. The binder drives gnatmake and reads the Ada spec, so the same declarations that make a routine callable also carry its range constraints into Jet.
comparisons.code: pragma Export (C, To_ECEF, "to_ecef");   -- C-ABI entry point

recommendation.why: Option A reuses the certified library through its own C-ABI exports, with no rewrite to re-certify. It reads range and constraint facts from the Ada spec, so an out-of-range Jet value is a checked error before the call. That pairs naturally with jet prove for the assurance-minded audience.
recommendation.tradeoff: The binder drives gnatmake and needs GNAT present, provisioned by jetpack. This mirrors the ratified Fortran gfortran model.

whyNot.reason: Option B hand-writes C shims and drops every Ada constraint. A latitude of 95 crosses silently and faults as Constraint_Error deep inside the Ada runtime, surfacing as a foreign crash rather than a clean Jet diagnostic.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship A. The GNAT binder that transports Ada's range constraints into checked Jet boundaries is the default. There is no separate hand-shim tier, because B's manual path is exactly what the binder removes.

harvest.use: the shipped ada.* surface with range facts and jet prove
the #Extern overlay under #Unsafe still exists for a symbol the binder cannot see, never as the default

decisions.title: Delphi / Object Pascal binder (the long-lived business-app estate)
decisions.gist: How Jet calls Delphi business rules in place and migrates the estate gradually.
decisions.lesson:
Object Pascal is the language behind Delphi, a long-standing tool for business desktop applications.

Delphi apps run inventory, billing, and scheduling at many companies for decades. Such apps are called LOB, meaning line-of-business.

FreePascal is the open-source Object Pascal compiler. cdecl is the plain C calling convention it can export.

An opaque handle is a reference to a foreign object whose internals Jet never inspects.
decisions.story:
Roy Anderson maintains a twenty-year-old Delphi inventory system. Its pricing and stock rules are correct and battle-tested, but the desktop UI is dated.

The company wants a new Jet web front end. Roy needs it to call the existing Delphi business rules in place, not reimplement them and risk changing a number.
decisions.inWild:
use pascal.inventory as inv

price :: inv.net_price(sku: "A-118", qty: 40)?

options.name: FreePascal C-ABI binder, classes as opaque handles
options.detail: Bind Object Pascal through FreePascal's cdecl exports. Classes become opaque handles, reusing the ratified C++ model but shallower, with no templates. The long-lived LOB estate gets a call-in-place surface today, and the same binder underwrites gradual migration through D-MIGRATE-SRC1.

options.name: No root — rewrite big-bang or stay
options.detail: Ship no `pascal` root. The company either reimplements twenty years of rules in Jet all at once or keeps the dated Delphi desktop app. There is no call-in-place path and no gradual migration.
options.code:
$ jet build
error[E3299]: no `pascal` binder — the Delphi rules are not reachable
  = help: reimplement the rules in Jet, or keep the Delphi app as-is

comparisons.note: FreePascal exports routines with the cdecl convention, so its compiled units link like any C library. The binder wraps those exports and models classes as opaque handles, the same shape the ratified C++ binder uses without templates.
comparisons.code: function NetPrice(Qty: Integer): Currency; cdecl; export;

recommendation.why: Option A calls the battle-tested Delphi rules in place, so no number changes and nothing is re-verified by hand. Classes become opaque handles, reusing the ratified C++ model without templates. The same binder underwrites gradual migration through D-MIGRATE-SRC1, so the estate moves file by file at its own pace.
recommendation.tradeoff: The binder needs FreePascal to compile the cdecl shims, provisioned by jetpack. A Delphi-only unit may need a small FreePascal-compatible export shim.

whyNot.reason: Option B offers no reachable path, so the company either rewrites twenty years of rules big-bang or keeps the dated desktop app forever. A rewrite risks changing a value the business depends on being exact.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship A. The FreePascal C-ABI binder gives call-in-place today and a gradual migration path through the shared source importer. There is no B tier, because its rewrite-or-stay is precisely the trap the binder removes.

harvest.use: the shipped pascal.* binder joined to D-MIGRATE-SRC1
still available later as the finish line of a D-MIGRATE-SRC1 migration, never forced up front

decisions.title: Database read/write leaves: how a live query proves it only reads
decisions.gist: Whether a database query proves it only reads data, so a live view can trust it — and whether a hidden write inside it gets caught.
decisions.lesson:
Three terms matter here. An effect row is the list of ambient powers, like network or database access, that Jet proves a function uses. A root is one of the ten built-in categories — Db, Fs, Net, and so on. A leaf is a narrower path under a root, like Db.Read or Db.Write, that a person writes to promise a function only reads or only writes.

Card #505 ratified app.live: it only accepts a query whose effect row sits inside Db.Read. Card #181 ratified a separate rule: leaf precision is a fact the compiler only trusts when a person writes it. It is never inferred from a real call. Every real call to core.db is tagged with the plain Db root, nothing finer. So no real query can satisfy the first rule today.
decisions.story: Frank writes the exact query D-LIVEQUERY1 promised: a function bound to Db.Read, calling db.query. He runs jet check and it fails — his function's real effect is the plain Db root, not the Db.Read leaf his signature demands. He reads both ratified decisions and neither one is wrong. They just can't both be followed at once.
decisions.detail:
Separate finding, same investigation: D-LIVEQUERY1's own worked example stacks @Pure on top of #(Db.Read). That combination already fails E0745 today — a @Pure fn asserts the empty effect set, and any #(...) bound asserts a non-empty one, so the two contradict by design.

Every option below drops the redundant @Pure marker and qualifies a live query by its #(Db.Read) bound alone, since a checked bound already proves nothing but permitted reads happen. This isn't a new choice — it's the only spelling that compiles under existing, unrelated law — but it changes the ratified inWild code, so it's called out here for visibility.

options.name: Infer Db.Read / Db.Write from core.db's own known methods
options.detail:
core.db has a small, closed method list: query and query_one always run a SELECT; execute runs arbitrary DDL or DML text. This ballot teaches the compiler's Core-call table to tag query and query_one with the leaf Db.Read, and execute with the leaf Db.Write. Connection lifecycle calls — begin, commit, rollback, close — keep the plain Db root, since they neither read nor write rows themselves.

This only touches the finite table the compiler already keeps for its own known standard-library signatures. It does not change how effects are inferred through ordinary user function calls, which stays bare-root only, exactly as D-EFFTREE1 already decided. A query fn that also sneaks in a write is now caught by the existing E0740 check, with no new diagnostic code.

options.name: Widen app.live's own gate to accept the plain Db root
options.detail:
app.live stops asking for the Db.Read leaf and instead accepts any function whose effect row is inside the plain Db root. No change to core_effect or the E0740 check is needed anywhere. A developer writes #(Db) instead of #(Db.Read), and any real database call — read or write — satisfies it.

The hole: nothing in sema catches a write hiding inside a query admitted this way. #Transact only tracks writes made inside its own block, and a live query runs outside one. Every reactive re-run of that query would fire the write again, with no rollback and no invalidation record.

options.name: Keep Db.Read in the law, but trust the annotation instead of checking it
options.detail:
D-LIVEQUERY1's wording stays exactly as ratified: app.live still asks for #(Db.Read). What changes is E0740 itself: when a real call only ever proves the plain Db root, a declared leaf bound under that root is accepted on sight, not verified. The person's #(Db.Read) becomes a promise the compiler prints back, not one it checks.

A query that writes still declares Db.Read and still gets waved through, same hole as widening the gate. The difference is cosmetic: the source now reads like a checked, safe contract when it never was one. A reviewer trusts a lie that looks like proof.
options.code:
#(Db.Read)
fn open_tickets_or_worse(team: Id<Team>) -> [Ticket] {
    db.execute("UPDATE tickets SET seen = true WHERE team = {team}", [])?
    return db.query("SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE team = {team}", [])?
}

tickets :: app.live(open_tickets_or_worse, team)

$ jet check app.jet
    (no errors — #(Db.Read) is trusted as written, the write inside is never checked)

comparisons.note: rustc special-cases a small, closed list of compiler-known functions and treats every other call generically. This ballot copies that shape: a closed table of core.db methods, nothing about user-defined calls changes.
comparisons.code:
// rustc knows mem::transmute, ptr::read, and friends by name —
// not by re-deriving their safety from generic analysis of a body.

recommendation.why: A is the only option where #(Db.Read) is actually true. It reuses E0740, a check that already exists, against a finite, compiler-authored table the same shape as the rest of core_effect.

whyNot.reason: Widening the gate removes the one property that makes a live query safe to re-run automatically: that it cannot mutate state. Nothing else in the language would catch a hidden write.
An unchecked contract is worse than no contract: it looks reviewed, so a reviewer stops looking for the bug the checked version would have caught for free.

recommendation.tradeoff: The amendment only covers core.db's own methods. A future feature that wants the same proof for Fs or Net needs its own ballot naming its exact methods, not a blanket rule.

hybrid.synthesis: There is no beginner/expert split here — a wrong safety proof is bad for everyone. A is the whole answer; B and C don't survive as expert options because they're the same hole with different cosmetics.

harvest.aspect: closed-table leaf inference for core.db's own methods
harvest.use: the whole mechanism — no split needed

harvest.aspect: a bare-Db gate admits any real database call
harvest.use: not used — it reopens the write-hole this ballot exists to close

harvest.aspect: the ratified Db.Read wording stays untouched
harvest.use: not used — A keeps that exact wording anyway, but makes it true instead of trusted

decisions.title: The error shape decode<T>() returns when a validate block fails
decisions.gist: When decode<T>() auto-runs a struct's validate block, what value does the caller's error arm hold if more than one rule fails.
decisions.lesson:
Decoding is turning raw bytes (JSON, YAML, a CSV row, …) into a typed Jet value. `json.decode<Signup>(text)` is the call every format shares.

A field error is a small record — a field path plus a plain-language reason, like `{path: "email", reason: "email required"}`. `DecodeError` is the type Jet has always used to report why a decode failed. It carries one path, one reason, one problem.

A validate block, just ratified as D-VALIDATE1, lets a struct declare rules next to its fields. One example rule: `check(password.len() >= 12, at: password, "needs at least 12 characters")`. Unlike a plain decode failure, a validate block runs every rule and collects every failure into a list. A signup form can then show "email required" AND "password too short" at once, instead of making the user fix one mistake, resubmit, and discover the next.

D-VALIDATE1 also said `decode<T>()` runs a type's validate block automatically, with no extra call needed. That is where the two designs collide. Decoding has always handed back ONE error, and validation now produces a LIST — something has to give, and only the owner can say what.

This matters because `decode<T>()` is the single most common way malformed data enters a Jet program: a web form, an API request body, a config file. Whatever it returns on failure is what nearly every Jet program's error-handling code gets written against.
decisions.story:
Priya is building a signup endpoint. A request comes in with a blank email and an 8-character password. She calls `json.decode<Signup>(body)` and wants to send the browser back every field that's wrong at once, so the user isn't stuck resubmitting three times to find all their mistakes.

She writes a `match` on the result and needs to know: is the error she gets back a single `DecodeError` like decoding has always produced? Or something new that can carry a whole list of field problems?
decisions.inWild: A `Signup` struct with a `validate` block, decoded straight from an HTTP request body: `json.decode<Signup>(req.body())`. The JSON has two problems at once — an empty email and a too-short password — and the handler wants to report both in one response.

options.name: DecodeError becomes one type with an accumulated case
options.detail:
`DecodeError` — the type every decode path already returns — turns from a plain path+reason record into a type with two shapes. One shape is the ordinary single-cause failure decoding has always produced (missing field, wrong type); the other is a new list-of-field-problems failure for a validate block. Every function that already promised `? DecodeError` keeps that promise; nothing about a function's declared error type changes.

The cost: `DecodeError` is used everywhere decoding happens today, not just inside `decode<T>()` — including a struct field's low-level `.field()`/`.int()`/`.text()` reads, and any hand-written decoder that builds a `DecodeError` directly. All of that code stops being a plain path+reason record and must be updated to handle the new second shape, even on types that never declare a validate block.
options.technical: `DecodeError` becomes a variant type: one arm keeps today's `{path, reason}` shape (parse/shape failure — decoding source data was structurally wrong); a second arm carries `[FieldError]` (validate block failure — the data parsed fine but broke a rule). `fn jet_decode(tree) -> Result<Self, DecodeError>` is unchanged; only what fills the `Err` side is new. Every existing `DecodeError.{ path: …, reason: … }` construction (hand-written `Decode` implementations included) must be rewritten as the new variant's spelling.

options.name: decode<T>() returns a new outcome type; DecodeError stays untouched
options.detail:
`decode<T>()` alone gets a new return type that can hold either shape of failure. `DecodeError` itself is not touched at all — the type every other decode path (`.field()`, `.int()`, hand-written decoders) already returns stays exactly the plain path+reason record it is today.

The reader gets the same benefit as option A: a struct's validate block failure shows every field problem at once through the ordinary `decode<T>()` call. But only code that actually calls `decode<T>()` on a validate-carrying type ever has to think about the new shape. Everything that reads a raw `DecodeError` today keeps compiling unchanged.
options.technical: A new type — call it `DecodeOutcome` — with two arms: `Shape(DecodeError)` for today's parse/shape failure, `Invalid([FieldError])` for a validate block's accumulated failures. `decode<T>()`'s signature becomes `Result<T, DecodeOutcome>`; every other decode-surface function (`DataTree.field/.at/.int/.text/.bool/.float`, the `Decode` trait itself, hand-written decoders) is untouched — `DecodeError` keeps its current plain-record shape everywhere else.

options.name: decode<T>() stops at the first failing rule
options.detail:
`DecodeError` never changes shape. `decode<T>()` still runs the validate block automatically, but the moment one rule fails, decoding stops right there and hands back one ordinary `DecodeError`, exactly like a missing field does today. The full list of every failing rule is only available by calling `Type.validate(value)` (or `Validate.over(s)`) directly.

This keeps decoding's long-standing single-error contract completely untouched. But it also means the one call beginners reach for first — `decode<T>()` — quietly does NOT give the "see every problem at once" behavior a validate block exists for. A form built straight on `decode<T>()` shows the user one mistake, then the next, one resubmit at a time.
options.technical: `decode<T>()`'s auto-run calls the synthesized `validate` function but short-circuits its rule loop on the first failing `check`, wrapping it as an ordinary `DecodeError { path, reason }` instead of collecting into `[FieldError]`. `Type.validate(value) -> Self ? [FieldError]` (already shipped) is the only path that runs every rule and returns the full list.

comparisons.note: Zod's `safeParse` always returns every issue at once, in one `ZodError` carrying an `issues` array — one result type, whether the input was shapeless JSON or a well-shaped value that failed a refinement. Closest in spirit to option A: one error type covers both failure classes.
comparisons.code:
const r = Signup.safeParse(body);
if (!r.success) r.error.issues.forEach(i => console.log(i.path, i.message));

comparisons.note: serde's `Deserialize` and the separate `validator` crate's `Validate` are two distinct traits with two distinct error types — a parse failure and a validation failure are never the same Result. Closest in spirit to option B: two failure classes, two types, joined only at the call site that runs both.
comparisons.code:
let v: Signup = serde_json::from_str(body)?;   // serde::Error
v.validate()?;                                  // validator::ValidationErrors

recommendation.why: It delivers the exact benefit a validate block exists for: decode<T>() on a Signup-shaped request shows every broken field at once, not one at a time. It touches only the one call site that needed to change. Every other place DecodeError already appears (DataTree.field()/.int()/.text(), the Decode trait, hand-written decoders) keeps working exactly as written today.

whyNot.reason: Turning DecodeError itself into a two-shaped type reaches far past decode<T>(). It reaches every low-level decode read and every hand-written Decode implementation that builds a DecodeError directly, including one already shipped as an example, even on types with no validate block at all. A change meant for one call site should not force every decode-surface user to learn a new shape.

The whole reason a validate block accumulates instead of stopping at the first failure is so a person fixes every mistake in one pass. Making decode<T>() stop at the first failing rule throws that away for the exact call beginners reach for first. It hides the real accumulating behavior behind a second, less obvious call (Type.validate).

recommendation.tradeoff: Every decode<T>() call now returns a slightly richer error — two arms instead of one — even for a type with no validate block, since the wrapping is uniform across every call. Code that used to read a bare DecodeError off decode<T>()'s failure arm now matches on which arm it is. That one small adjustment is what buys every validate-carrying type its full field-by-field error report for free.

hybrid.synthesis: B is the base. It carries A's real prize: a validate-carrying type's decode<T>() caller gets the exact same full accumulated field list Type.validate() would give, never a weaker one-at-a-time report. It also carries C's discipline of never touching the plain DecodeError record everywhere it already appears today. The new outcome type is uniform across every decode<T>() call, not only validate-carrying ones, because decode<T>() has one generic signature. Giving it a different return shape per type would be a deeper change than this ballot scopes.

harvest.aspect: One error value that accumulates every failing rule instead of stopping at the first.
harvest.use: Kept exactly — DecodeOutcome.Invalid([FieldError]) IS that accumulated value; only its home type changes (a new DecodeOutcome, not a mutated DecodeError).

harvest.aspect: A single new type scoped to decode<T>() alone, leaving the rest of the decode surface untouched.
harvest.use: Adopted as the mechanism.

harvest.aspect: The plain path+reason DecodeError record never changes shape anywhere it already appears.
harvest.use: Kept in full for every existing DecodeError use: DataTree.field()/.int()/.text(), hand-written decoders. C's other idea — widening decode<T>()'s result only for validate-carrying types — cannot fit decode<T>()'s single generic signature without a different type per struct. Only the untouched-DecodeError half survives into B.

decisions.title: Whether validate blocks get a built-in rule vocabulary beyond check()
decisions.gist: Whether common per-field rules like "is an email" or "at least N characters" get their own short spelling, or every rule stays a hand-written check() condition.
decisions.lesson:
A validate block, ratified as D-VALIDATE1, is a section inside a struct that lists rules a value must satisfy. Today it holds only one kind of statement: `check(condition, at: field, "message")`. `condition` is any true/false expression. `at:` names the field the failure is reported against, and the string is the message shown to the user.

A rule vocabulary means short, purpose-built spellings for rules that come up constantly, like is this text an email address, or is this string at least N characters long. Instead of writing that boolean logic by hand every time, a name like `.email()` or `.min_len(12)` says it directly.

A canned message is text the compiler supplies automatically when a named rule fails, instead of the user typing their own string. "must be a valid email address" is a canned message; "email required" is a hand-written one.

This matters because check() by itself works for any rule, but every field-level rule becomes its own from-scratch boolean expression and its own hand-typed message, no matter how common the rule is. The struct definition is Jet's one schema — whatever this decision picks becomes how every Jet program spells its most common data rules.
decisions.story:
Devon is writing a Signup struct with fields most apps have: an email that must look like an email, and a password with a minimum length. He types `check(email.len() > 0, at: email, "email required")`. He realizes he will retype some version of this same boolean logic in every struct with an email field, in every project, for as long as he uses Jet.

He wants to know: does Jet give these everyday rules a name, or does every project keep hand-rolling the same handful of conditions?
decisions.inWild: A Signup struct with an email field and a password field, each needing the same few rules most forms need: the email must be present and look like an email, the password must meet a minimum length, and the password must not equal the email.

options.name: Closed starter vocabulary with canned messages
options.detail:
A small, fixed set of dot-chain rule methods ships on bare field names inside a validate block: `.not_empty()`, `.email()`, `.min_len(n)`, `.max_len(n)`, `.has_digit()`. Each expands to an ordinary check() call with a message the compiler supplies. Cross-field rules keep using check() directly, exactly as today.

The list is closed — a fixed set the owner ratifies once, not an open plugin surface. Adding a new rule name later needs its own ballot, the same way Jet's other closed vocabularies work today (the blessed-abbreviation list, the ambient-surface registry).
options.technical: Each vocabulary method is sugar: `email.email()` lowers to `check(core.validate.is_email(value.email), at: email, "must be a valid email address")`, so it shares the exact check()-based engine and [FieldError] accumulation D-VALIDATE1 already specified. No second engine, no second error type.

options.name: No vocabulary — check() is the one mechanism
options.detail:
Nothing new ships. Every rule, common or not, is a hand-written check() call with a hand-written condition and a hand-written message. This is exactly what card #506 already shipped.

One mechanism, no compiler-owned message text, nothing to ratify or extend later. The cost falls on every struct: the same email-shaped, length-bounded rules get retyped by hand in every project that needs them.
options.technical: No change to CheckerValidate.rs; the shipped `extract_check_rule` already requires every validate-block statement to be a `check(cond, at: field, "msg")` call, and this option keeps that the permanent, only shape.

options.name: Vocabulary as plain functions, used inside check()
options.detail:
A `core.validate` module ships plain, pure functions — `is_email(s)`, `has_min_len(s, n)`, `has_max_len(s, n)`, `has_digit(s)` — each returning true or false. They are ordinary function calls a user composes inside a check() condition. No new statement shape, no canned message; the user still writes every message by hand.

check() stays the one and only statement a validate block accepts. The vocabulary only saves the work of writing the boolean logic, not the check()/at:/message ceremony around it.
options.technical: `core.validate.is_email`, `.has_min_len`, `.has_max_len`, `.has_digit` are ordinary `@Pure` functions in a stdlib module, callable anywhere a Bool expression is legal, including a check() condition and Validate.over(s)'s chain. No parser or CheckerValidate.rs change beyond exposing the module.

comparisons.note: Pydantic ships named field constraints (EmailStr, Field(min_length=12)) with built-in messages, then lets a custom validator add anything the constraint set can't express. Closest to option A: a closed named vocabulary plus an escape hatch.

Zod's `.email()`/`.min(12)` chain methods are themselves built from small reusable refinement functions under the hood, while every custom rule is still a plain predicate passed to `.refine()`. Closest to option C's engine, wrapped in option A's chain sugar.
comparisons.code:
z.string().email().min(12)
z.string().refine(s => isEmail(s), "must be a valid email address")

recommendation.why: D-VALIDATE1's own ratified text already describes rules as "dot-chains on bare field names," with check() reserved for cross-field rules. Option A is what finishes that promise. It also matches how Jet already closes off small vocabularies elsewhere — the blessed-abbreviation list, the ambient-surface registry — ratified once, extended only by a future ballot.

whyNot.reason: Leaving every field-level rule as hand-rolled boolean logic backs away from the dot-chain spelling D-VALIDATE1's own text already committed to. It also keeps the exact repetition Jet strips out elsewhere in the language, like inferred constructors and inherited fields.

The predicate functions cut only the condition-writing work. Every rule still needs its own full check(condition, at: field, "message") wrapper, so the field-name and message ceremony D-VALIDATE1's dot-chain spelling was meant to remove is still there on every line.

recommendation.tradeoff: A canned message is generic where a hand-written one can be specific to the form it's on: is required, instead of email required. That is acceptable because check() still sits right there for any rule that needs its own wording. The vocabulary is only for the common case.

hybrid.synthesis: A is the base. check() stays exactly what B already ships: the always-available way to write any rule the vocabulary doesn't name, especially every cross-field rule. Underneath, each vocabulary method is C's idea in different clothes — a small pure predicate function, wired to a canned message and a check() call — so A ships one engine, not two.

harvest.aspect: Closed dot-chain vocabulary with canned messages.
harvest.use: Adopted as the user-facing surface.

harvest.aspect: check() as the one statement a validate block accepts.
harvest.use: Kept unchanged — the vocabulary only adds sugar in front of it; every cross-field and custom rule still writes check() directly.

harvest.aspect: Rule logic as plain, reusable pure functions rather than a new marker system.
harvest.use: Kept as the implementation underneath the sugar — each dot-chain method lowers to one of these functions inside an ordinary check() call, so the vocabulary adds no second engine.

decisions.title: Android native-widget and Kotlin interop transport
decisions.gist: How Jet's Android backend reaches native widgets and existing Kotlin libraries without creating a second UI model.
decisions.lesson:
Android applications normally contain Java or Kotlin code running on Android Runtime, plus optional native machine code. The Java Native Interface, or JNI, is Android's standard bridge between those worlds. Jet can compile its application logic to native code, then use JNI to create Android View widgets and receive lifecycle or input callbacks.

Jetpack Compose is Google's newer Kotlin UI toolkit. Compose builds screens from Kotlin functions instead of directly assembling classic View objects. A Compose bridge would generate Kotlin adapters that translate Jet's View tree into Compose calls. That translation must not become a second Jet component model.

The transport matters at two boundaries. Jet's own renderer needs predictable widget creation, updates, events, ownership, and errors. Experts also need access to existing Android libraries whose public APIs are Kotlin or Java. Jet already ratified one `java.*` binder over JNI. This decision chooses whether the Android UI backend uses that common binder directly, adds a Compose-specific adapter, or exposes both behind one backend contract.

For example, a Jet Button remains one Jet Button on every platform. On Android, the chosen transport decides whether its backend creates `android.widget.Button`, calls generated Compose code, or selects either implementation behind the same backend interface. User application code and reactive state remain unchanged.
decisions.story: Mina moves a Jet inventory app from Linux to Android. Its shared screen contains a search field, list, and camera button. She wants standard Android accessibility and lifecycle behavior. Her company also has a Kotlin barcode-scanner library. Mina should keep one Jet screen while still calling that library through a typed, inspectable boundary.

options.name: Direct JNI View backend
options.detail: Jet's Android backend uses generated JNI bindings to Android's classic View toolkit. The same java.* binder projects third-party Kotlin and Java libraries. Every callback crosses one typed boundary with checked ownership and Jet diagnostics. Experts can inspect generated bindings and override provisioned SDK or NDK handles. Compose-only libraries need an explicit Kotlin adapter package.
options.technical: Package a native shared library inside a minimal Android application shell. Generated JNI entrypoints attach to the existing Android Runtime, retain Java objects as opaque owned handles, and lower exceptions to JavaError. UI operations implement the existing JetBackend seam. No second embedded JVM is started on Android.
options.code:
$ jet inspect bind java android.widget.Button
+projected  android.widget.Button -> java.android.widget.Button
+transport  existing Android Runtime via JNI
+
+$ jet build --target=android
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+backend    android-view / JNI
+
+error: Compose-only type `CameraPreview` has no Android View entrypoint
+  fix: add a Kotlin adapter that exposes a View, or choose the Compose-capable transport

options.name: Generated Kotlin Compose bridge
options.detail: Jet generates a Kotlin layer that renders its View tree through Compose. Existing Compose libraries fit naturally, and Android previews see generated Kotlin components. Classic View libraries require Compose interop wrappers. Experts can inspect and pin generated Kotlin, Gradle, compiler-plugin, and SDK inputs. The generated layer adds a platform-specific translation between Jet and native widgets.
options.technical: Jet emits Kotlin composables plus JNI calls into the native Jet state engine. State identity remains owned by Jet; Compose observes snapshots and returns events. Generated Kotlin is derived output, never an editable source of truth.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android --android-backend=compose
+generated  target/android/generated/JetInventory.kt
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+backend    compose / generated Kotlin bridge
+
+$ jet inspect generated android
+JetInventory.kt  hash:7ad2...  source:InventoryView

options.name: One Android backend protocol with View default and Compose adapter
options.detail: Jet keeps one Android backend contract. Its ceremony-free default uses direct JNI Views. A project may select the first-party Compose adapter without changing Jet components, state, events, or accessibility semantics. The same java.* binder handles ordinary Kotlin and Java libraries in both modes. Experts control the backend, generated adapters, toolchain, cache, and audit output through package policy.
options.technical: Define one AndroidBackend implementation contract under JetBackend. AndroidViewBackend is the default. AndroidComposeBackend consumes the identical checked UI tree and event protocol. Conformance tests require matching tree semantics, state identity, lifecycle restoration, accessibility facts, and diagnostics. Backend selection is build policy, not new language syntax.
options.code:
$ jet build --target=android
+backend    android-view (default)
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+
+$ jet build --target=android --android-backend=compose
+backend    android-compose (same checked View tree)
+built      target/android/inventory.aab
+
+$ jet inspect android --audit
+ui-model   core.ui/View
+transport  JNI + generated Compose adapter
+toolchain  android-ndk r27, Kotlin 2.2, hashes recorded

comparisons.note: Flutter keeps one Dart widget model while platform channels reach Kotlin APIs. Its default renderer owns pixels, unlike Jet's ratified native-widget direction.
comparisons.code:
const channel = MethodChannel('scanner');
+final code = await channel.invokeMethod('scan');

comparisons.note: React Native maps one component model to Android views and also permits native modules. Its generated architecture shows why UI transport and library interop should share typed metadata.

recommendation.why: C preserves the ratified native-widget default while letting Compose ecosystems participate through a conforming adapter. One checked View tree and one java.* binder serve beginners and experts.

whyNot.reason: A makes Compose-only libraries require bespoke wrappers even though a reusable conforming adapter can preserve Jet semantics.
B makes a generated Compose translation mandatory and weakens the direct platform-widget default ratified by D-NATIVEUI1.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two backend implementations require parity enforcement. Shared conformance tests and one checked tree make that duplication an implementation detail, not a second user model.

hybrid.synthesis: C keeps A's direct JNI View path as the default and adds B's Compose access as a selectable adapter over the identical backend protocol. Library calls use the ratified java.* binder in either mode.

harvest.aspect: Direct native View access with one typed JNI boundary.
harvest.use: Use it as the default Android backend and common Kotlin or Java interop transport.

harvest.aspect: Natural access to Compose-only widgets and libraries.
harvest.use: Provide it as a first-party conforming adapter whose generated Kotlin remains derived and auditable.

harvest.aspect: One public UI model across transport choices.
harvest.use: Make backend conformance and identical Jet source the binding rule.

decisions.title: Native UI hot reload and component preview model
decisions.gist: How `jet dev` updates running native apps and previews components while preserving one runtime model.
decisions.lesson:
A native hot reload loop changes a running application after source is saved. A plain restart rebuilds and launches again, losing temporary state. A hot swap replaces checked executable units inside a resident process, then reconciles the existing widget tree with the new View tree.

State identity decides what survives. Jet already ratified `@Persist`: a marked module binding survives `jet dev` reload when its module path, name, and compatible value shape still match. Ordinary local state may reset. Widget identity also needs stable source-derived keys so a changed label updates the existing native widget instead of opening another window.

A component preview renders one component with chosen sample inputs, device size, theme, locale, and accessibility settings. It can run inside a separate preview host or inside the same resident runtime used by the full app. A shared host gives previews the same layout, event, lifecycle, and backend behavior as the application.

This choice controls trust as well as speed. Reloaded code must pass the normal parser, semantic checks, and executable TIR pipeline before entering the process. A failed change leaves the last good app running and shows a Jet diagnostic. No native linker or platform-tool error should leak to the user.
decisions.story: Luis adjusts a checkout screen while it runs on an Android phone and an iPhone simulator. He has already filled a long form. Saving a color change should keep the form values, update both native widget trees, and show the same component under large text. A bad edit should leave the last good screen usable.

options.name: Full-app state-preserving hot reload
options.detail: `jet dev --target=ios|android` runs the complete app in a resident native host. Each valid save swaps changed checked modules and reconciles native widgets. `@Persist` state survives by its ratified identity rules. Beginners use one command. Experts inspect swap units, state migration, backend calls, hashes, timing, and fallback reasons. Component previews are ordinary small applications.
options.technical: Reuse checked TIR and the resident JIT or platform dynamic-loading boundary. Compute a module dependency closure, validate ABI and value layouts before activation, apply the swap atomically, then diff the View tree. Unsupported native changes trigger a diagnosed controlled restart, never partial mutation.
options.code:
$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=android
+ready    Pixel 10 / android-view
+changed  CheckoutView
+checked  18 ms
+swapped  7 ms; widgets reused: 12; created: 1
+state    persisted: cart
+
+error E2204: this edit changes a native boundary
+  what: Scanner.scan now returns a different type
+  fix:  Jet kept the last good app running; press `r` for a controlled restart

options.name: Isolated component preview host
options.detail: `jet preview` runs selected components in a dedicated native host with sample inputs and device traits. Changes reload only the preview graph. This makes themes, sizes, locales, focus, and accessibility states explicit. Full applications still rebuild and restart, so navigation, lifecycle, restoration, and cross-component behavior are not exercised in the fast loop.
options.technical: The preview host loads checked component entrypoints and fixture values. It uses the production backend and renderer, but substitutes lifecycle, navigation, storage, and external effects with declared preview capabilities.
options.code:
$ jet preview checkout.jet CheckoutView --target=ios
+preview  iPhone 17 Pro, light, en-US
+
+keys: d device  t theme  l locale  a accessibility  q quit
+saved    component reloaded; app navigation not running
+
+$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=ios
+note: native full-app changes rebuild and restart

options.name: One resident native dev host for apps and previews
options.detail: `jet dev` owns one resident runtime and checked swap protocol. Full-app mode is the ceremony-free default. A preview selector narrows the root component and adds device, theme, locale, lifecycle, and accessibility controls. Both modes use production backends, identical state identity, and the same diagnostics. Experts control swap policy, restart boundaries, devices, capabilities, scheduling, caches, and audit receipts.
options.technical: Model app and preview as root configurations for one NativeDevHost. Every edit passes parser, sema, TIR validation, ABI checks, atomic activation, View reconciliation, and state migration. Preview capabilities are explicit inputs, not mocks hidden in component code. Device and simulator transports carry signed swap bundles and receipts.
options.code:
$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=android
+mode     app; device: Pixel 10
+saved    swapped 2 modules; persisted: cart
+
+$ jet dev checkout.jet --target=ios --preview=CheckoutView
+mode     preview; device: iPhone 17 Pro; theme: light; locale: en-US
+keys     d device  t theme  l locale  a accessibility
+saved    same swap protocol; widgets reused: 12
+
+$ jet inspect dev --audit
+source  CheckoutView@9f31...
+tir     checked@31aa...
+device  simulator-4A2D
+swap    atomic; fallback:none

comparisons.note: Flutter combines stateful full-app hot reload with widget-focused development. Its resident VM shows the value of preserving state while rebuilding the UI tree.
comparisons.code:
$ flutter run
r Hot reload.
R Hot restart.

comparisons.note: Both provide component previews with device and environment controls. Their previews can differ from full application lifecycle behavior, which argues for one Jet host and protocol.

recommendation.why: C gives beginners one real application loop and gives experts precise preview controls without inventing a second renderer or runtime. It directly fulfills D-PERSIST1 through one checked swap protocol.

whyNot.reason: A preserves real application behavior but treats focused previews as disposable mini-apps without first-class environment controls.
B improves component iteration while leaving the full native application loop restart-only and unable to prove lifecycle parity.

recommendation.tradeoff: The resident host becomes a security and correctness boundary. Mandatory semantic checks, atomic activation, signed device transport, and last-good rollback keep that boundary explicit and auditable.

hybrid.synthesis: C uses A's real full-app resident loop and B's focused environment controls as two root configurations of the same checked native host. Production backends and state rules remain identical.

harvest.aspect: State-preserving edits inside the actual application.
harvest.use: Make full-app hot reload the default `jet dev` mode.

harvest.aspect: Fast component isolation across device and accessibility environments.
harvest.use: Add preview roots and explicit environment inputs to the same host.

harvest.aspect: One swap protocol and one production renderer.
harvest.use: Require app and preview modes to share validation, activation, reconciliation, and audit receipts.

decisions.title: Mobile platform work deferred
decisions.outcome: Defer mobile-native platform work; current burndown focuses the Jet language and Linux support.
decisions.comment: Defer mobile-native platform work; current burndown focuses the Jet language and Linux support.

decisions.title: Semantics of the seven hangar operational verbs
decisions.gist: What repair, copy, import, export, dump, restore, and sign actually do inside the hangar.
decisions.lesson: The hangar is a content-addressed, generational package store. Every realized package is an object named by its content digest; an object plus everything it references is a closure. These seven verbs are the store's integrity, portability, and trust surface. Words are ratified (D-CLI-STORE2=A). This ballot fixes their behavior. Every mutation is plan-before-apply with stable JSON, and every import is verified then quarantined before it counts (D-JPK-STORECLI1=D). The one open design question is whether serialization needs two concepts or one.
decisions.story: Maya runs an air-gapped CI box. On her networked laptop she realizes imaging@2.4.0 into the hangar. She must move that object and everything it references onto the offline box, prove nothing was tampered with, and make the box trust it. A week later a disk fault corrupts one object. She needs it whole again without rebuilding the world.
decisions.inWild: Maya's hangar holds `imaging-2.4.0-a91f` plus five references. `jet hangar verify` (already built) reports `imaging-2.4.0-a91f failed its content digest`. She has no network on the target box, so she must serialize the closure to a file, hand-carry it, and sign it so the offline box will register it. The ratified surface promises `export`, `import`, `dump`, `restore`, `copy`, `sign`, and `repair` for exactly this loop. Today each prints an honest `not yet built`.

options.name: Nix-faithful: one primitive per verb
options.detail: Each verb maps 1:1 to a nix-store operation. dump and restore serialize a single object as a raw stream, no closure and no signature. export and import carry the closure plus references plus signatures. copy is the live endpoint transfer. repair re-realizes. sign attaches a detached signature. Power users transfer Nix knowledge directly. Cost: dump-archive and export-archive are two serialization concepts a user must learn to tell apart.
options.code:
# laptop: serialize the imaging closure to a file, hand-carry it
$ jet hangar export imaging@2.4.0 --to imaging.closure
exported 6 objects (imaging + 5 references) -> imaging.closure (48 MB)

# air-gapped box: import verifies signatures, quarantines, then registers
$ jet hangar import imaging.closure
imported 6 objects into quarantine; 6/6 content digests OK
registered imaging-2.4.0-a91f into the hangar

# a single object, no closure, raw stream (nix-store --dump/--restore twin)
$ jet hangar dump imaging-2.4.0-a91f | ssh box jet hangar restore
restored 1 object (no references resolved)

# live store-to-store, no intermediate file
$ jet hangar copy imaging@2.4.0 --to ssh://box
copied 6 objects to ssh://box

# corruption: re-realize the broken object from its recipe
$ jet hangar repair imaging-2.4.0-a91f
imaging-2.4.0-a91f failed its digest; re-realized from recipe; OK

# trust: attach a detached signature
$ jet hangar sign imaging-2.4.0-a91f --key ci
signed imaging-2.4.0-a91f with key `ci`

# the friction: `dump` and `export` are two archive concepts.
# A user who reaches for `dump imaging@2.4.0` silently loses the closure.

options.name: Unified archive backbone: one format, seven ergonomic views
options.detail: One canonical, signed, self-describing `.hangar` archive. export writes it to a file, closure by default, with --no-deps for a leaf. import verifies and quarantines it. dump and restore are the stdin/stdout streaming twins that emit the same bytes. copy fuses export, transport, and import over an endpoint. repair verifies then re-realizes or re-fetches. sign (re)signs an object or archive. Beginners stop at export and import. Experts pipe dump and target copy --to ssh://. No verb invents a second serialization concept.
options.code:
# ONE archive format. export writes it, closure by default. Beginners stop here.
$ jet hangar export imaging@2.4.0 --to imaging.hangar
plan:  6 objects, signed by `ci`, 48 MB -> imaging.hangar
apply: wrote imaging.hangar

# a single object is the SAME format, just fewer objects
$ jet hangar export imaging@2.4.0 --no-deps --to leaf.hangar
plan:  1 object -> leaf.hangar
apply: wrote leaf.hangar

# import: same format, verified + quarantined before it counts
$ jet hangar import imaging.hangar
plan:  6 objects; signatures OK; 6/6 digests OK
apply: registered imaging-2.4.0-a91f (+5 refs)

# dump/restore = the same archive, streamed instead of filed (expert pipe)
$ jet hangar dump imaging@2.4.0 | ssh box jet hangar restore
apply: registered imaging-2.4.0-a91f (+5 refs)

# copy = export -> transport -> import, fused over an endpoint
$ jet hangar copy imaging@2.4.0 --to ssh://box
plan:  6 objects -> ssh://box (2 already present)
apply: transferred 4 objects; box verified 6/6

# repair = verify, then re-realize or re-fetch the broken object
$ jet hangar repair imaging-2.4.0-a91f
imaging-2.4.0-a91f failed its digest; re-realized from recipe; verified OK

# sign = (re)sign an object or an archive with a key
$ jet hangar sign imaging@2.4.0 --key ci
signed imaging-2.4.0-a91f with key `ci`

options.name: Acceptance-scoped: build the two workflows in use, defer the rest
options.detail: Implement only what jetos owner-parity needs today: repair, and the export/import closure archive. copy, dump, restore, and sign stay honest teaching errors that name the working path, until a ratified workflow demands them. The default surface stays small and nothing ships half-built. Cost: four ratified verb words sit dark, and a user reading the ratified surface meets gaps where the docs promised a verb.
options.code:
# what jetos parity needs today: repair + export/import (signed closure)
$ jet hangar export imaging@2.4.0 --to imaging.hangar
plan:  6 objects, signed by `ci` -> imaging.hangar
apply: wrote imaging.hangar

$ jet hangar import imaging.hangar
apply: registered imaging-2.4.0-a91f (+5 refs); 6/6 digests OK

$ jet hangar repair imaging-2.4.0-a91f
re-realized from recipe; verified OK

# the rest stay honest teaching errors until a real workflow needs them
$ jet hangar copy imaging@2.4.0 --to ssh://box
error: `jet hangar copy` is reserved but not built
  no ratified workflow needs store-to-store copy yet
  to move an object now: jet hangar export ... then import on the target

$ jet hangar dump imaging-2.4.0-a91f
error: `jet hangar dump` is reserved but not built
  for a single-object archive, use: jet hangar export --no-deps

comparisons.note: Nix splits single-path from closure serialization: --dump/--restore move one path as a raw NAR, while --export/--import carry the reference closure. Signing and repair are separate again. Option B unifies the two archive concepts; A preserves the split.
comparisons.code:
nix-store --export /nix/store/..-imaging | ssh box nix-store --import   # closure
nix-store --dump /nix/store/..-imaging  | ssh box nix-store --restore  # one path
nix store sign --key-file ci.key /nix/store/..-imaging
nix-store --verify --check-contents --repair

comparisons.note: guix archive folds single and closure export into one command with -r, and signing is mandatory: the target store refuses an unsigned import. This informs B's signed-by-default archive.
comparisons.code:
guix archive --generate-key
guix archive --export -r imaging | ssh box guix archive --import   # box rejects unsigned

comparisons.note: docker save/load is a flat layer tarball with no reference-closure model and content digests per layer. Signing is a separate trust subsystem. A hangar closure carries references Docker does not model.
comparisons.code:
docker save imaging:2.4.0 | ssh box docker load
docker trust sign imaging:2.4.0

comparisons.note: ostree is content-addressed like the hangar. fsck is the repair analog; commits are GPG-signed; pull-local moves refs between repos. Confirms repair = fsck + re-realize and sign = attach signature.
comparisons.code:
ostree fsck
ostree gpg-sign COMMIT KEYID
ostree pull-local /other/repo ref

recommendation.why: Option B. One signed, self-describing `.hangar` archive underlies all seven verbs. Beginners learn two words, export and import, and stop. Experts pipe dump, target copy --to an endpoint, and pass --no-deps for a leaf. Because dump and export emit identical bytes, there is exactly one way to mean serialize an object (I8), which kills the dump-versus-export confusion Nix carries. Every verb shares one verify, quarantine, and trust path, so integrity and signing behave the same everywhere. It keeps all ratified words and hollows nothing.
recommendation.tradeoff: All seven verbs stand on one archive format, so that format becomes a stability commitment. It needs a version field and a compatibility rule from day one, and repair and copy wait for the backbone to exist before they light up.

whyNot.reason: dump-archive and export-archive are two ways to serialize an object. That is a second way to mean the same job (I8 friction), and a user who reaches for dump silently loses the closure.
Leaves four ratified verbs dark as permanent teaching errors. The owner ratified the full surface; deferring most of it reads as a hollow default and a broken promise in the docs.

hybrid.synthesis: B is already the hybrid. The beginner surface is export and import, with closure and signing on by default and zero flags. The expert surface is the same mechanism reached differently. Dump and restore stream the identical archive over a pipe, copy fuses the round trip over an endpoint (D-JPK-STOREBACKEND1 adapters), and --no-deps narrows to a leaf. One archive format, one verify-and-quarantine gate, one signing model. The seven verbs are ergonomic entrypoints, never seven independent systems.

harvest.aspect: closure-by-default export and verified, quarantined import
harvest.use: kept as the default behavior of B's export and import

harvest.aspect: single signed .hangar archive behind all seven verbs
harvest.use: the shipped mechanism
implementation starts with the repair and export/import workflows jetos acceptance already needs

decisions.title: JWT/PASETO verify before the app graph
decisions.gist: Whether token verification ships as standalone functions now, or waits for the whole app graph.
decisions.lesson: A common, safe capability should not wait on unrelated infrastructure. Verifying a third-party token is useful long before Jet has an application graph.
decisions.story:
Priya runs an API gateway. A partner posts requests carrying a signed JWT, and she must reject any token whose signature, expiry, or audience is wrong before trusting the caller.

She does not want to stand up a full web app to do it. She wants one function that takes the token and the key and returns typed claims or a clear failure.

options.name: core.auth typed functions now
options.detail: Ship `core.auth` now with typed verify functions. `auth.verify_jwt(token, key)` returns `Result<Claims>` with expiry and audience already checked. When the app graph lands, `app.auth` calls these same functions, so there is one mechanism with two entrypoints.

options.name: Wait for the app graph (#438)
options.detail: Ship no standalone surface. Token verification exists only through `app.auth`, which rides the app graph. Until card #438 lands, naming the auth surface is a teaching stop that points to the pending card.
options.code:
use core.auth

fn handle(req: Request) -> Response {
  claims := auth.verify_jwt(req.bearer(), key: partner_key)?
  Response.ok(for: claims.subject)
}

# --- what Priya sees today under option B ---
#
#   $ jet build gateway.jet
#   Error [E0763]: token verification is not available yet
#     |-- gateway.jet:4
#     |   claims := auth.verify_jwt(req.bearer(), key: partner_key)?
