Best direct visible workspace root. TOML is easy to review; Rust makes the tools dependable.

recommendation.why: A gives the smallest beginning and the cleanest growth. The root stays obvious, while every split file remains a typed piece of the same project.

whyNot.reason: Guix grows beautifully, but Scheme modules and errors would make Jet projects feel foreign.
Cargo is clear, but a manifest in every member restores the repetition Jet should remove.
CUE splits effortlessly, but no root owns the whole project and another language becomes required.
Reserved role files force users to learn the build system before their project needs those roles.

recommendation.tradeoff: `project.jet` becomes a new canonical file and replaces current role filenames. The migration is worthwhile because it removes permanent ceremony.

decisions.comment: Ok with this conceptually but need a different word. Parts should be a convenience extensibility and modularity feature but a requirement

decisions.title: Callable contracts for runnable Outputs
decisions.gist: Choose how commands, services, and checks use ordinary functions.
decisions.lesson: Executable Outputs are user-invoked commands, so typed parameters can become checked flags through the ratified entry-parameter model. Services and checks run unattended; their settings belong in checked Package values. Every callable returns `Void` or `Void ?`. A service lives while its call lives. A check passes on normal return and fails on error.
decisions.story: Maya packages an export command, API service, and release check. CI and deployment must run the same service and check configuration as her laptop.
decisions.inWild: The proposal uses `fn export(path: Path)`, parameterless `fn serve()`, and parameterless `fn verify_release()`. Output values carry service and check settings rather than invocation flags.

options.name: Role-specific ordinary functions
options.detail: Commands may take typed parameters. Services and checks take none. Each returns `Void` or `Void ?`.
options.code:
fn export(path: Path) -> Void ?
$ jet run export --path out.json
fn serve() -> Void ?
fn verify() -> Void ?
$ jet test verify
PASS verify

options.name: One permissive shape
options.detail: Every runnable Output may take typed parameters, including services and checks.
options.code:
fn verify(channel: String = "stable") -> Void ?
$ jet test verify
PASS verify
$ jet test verify --channel nightly
PASS verify

options.name: Lifecycle result types
options.detail: Each role returns a tool-facing result type instead of ordinary completion or failure.

recommendation.why: Typed command flags remain ergonomic while unattended service and check configuration has one checked source in the Package graph.

whyNot.reason: Service and check flags create alternate configurations that local runs and automation may select differently.
Business code must construct tool protocol values instead of using normal return and error flow.

recommendation.tradeoff: Services and checks cannot accept ad hoc invocation flags; their settings must be represented in checked graph values.

decisions.title: Default Output selection
decisions.gist: Choose the deterministic selection rule for singular Output intents while plural test runs every Check.
decisions.lesson: `jet test` is plural and runs every Check Output. `run`, `enter`, `publish`, and activation need one Output. The ordered selection rule can use an explicit address, the unchanged function-only `fn run` path, a sole capable Output, or a checked `defaults:` entry. Adding a second candidate must never silently retarget automation.
decisions.story: Maya's Package begins with one command, so `jet run` needs no extra configuration. After she adds an administrator command, Jet must stop and ask for an explicit default rather than choosing a different command by accident.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's hobby Package declares `defaults: .{ run: app, check: unit, enter: dev }`. Explicit addresses always win, and plural `jet test` still runs every Check.

options.name: Plural all; ordered singular rule
options.detail: Use explicit address, unchanged `fn run`, sole capable Output, checked default, then sorted candidate error.
options.code:
$ jet test
PASS unit
PASS release

$ jet run
Selected sole Executable `cli`.

# after adding admin
$ jet run
Choose one Output: admin, cli
Fix: add defaults: .{ run: cli } or run an explicit address.

options.name: Conventional keys
options.detail: Reserve Output keys such as `run` and `check` as implicit defaults.

options.name: Always explicit after Outputs
options.detail: Require an Output address whenever any Outputs are declared, even when only one can satisfy the command.
options.code:
$ jet run
name an Output; use jet run cli

recommendation.why: Small Packages stay automatic, larger Packages record checked intent, and a new Output cannot silently retarget an existing command.

whyNot.reason: Conventional keys turn ordinary Output names into reserved policy vocabulary.
Naming a sole capable Output adds typing without adding information.

recommendation.tradeoff: A Package with several Outputs for one singular capability carries a small `defaults:` record.

decisions.title: Facts stored in each Output value
decisions.gist: Decide whether Output values are thin typed projections or repeat graph slices.
decisions.lesson: An Output is a named result selected from one Package graph. Thin projection means the Output stores only its name and kind-specific facts. Sources, dependencies, actions, effects, policy, target facts, and provenance stay single-copy on the graph. `jet inspect output` reconstructs the complete path for audit.
decisions.story: Maya publishes a command and an image built from that command. She changes the command's source set once and expects both outputs and their audit views to use the same fact.
decisions.inWild: The proposal shows `todo.cli` as a small Executable value. `jet inspect output todo.cli` expands its source set, dependencies, action digest, target, effects, policy, and provenance from the Package graph.

options.name: Thin projections
options.detail: Outputs hold only name and kind-specific facts. Inspection reconstructs the complete path from the Package graph.

options.name: Explicit slice per Output
options.detail: Every Output repeats its source, dependency, action, and policy references.
options.code: cli: Output :: .Executable.{ name: "todo", entry: run, sources: [app], deps: [textkit], actions: [compile], policy: release }

options.name: Verb sections
options.detail: Each Output divides repeated facts into build, run, and publish sections.
options.code: cli: Output :: .Executable.{ name: "todo", build: .{ actions: [compile] }, run: .{ entry: run }, publish: .{ policy: release } }

recommendation.why: Facts remain single-copy and Output declarations stay readable while one inspect view supplies the full audit path.

whyNot.reason: Every Output repeats references that can disagree with the Package graph or another Output.
Stable facts become scattered by command verb and still repeat across Outputs.

recommendation.tradeoff: An isolated Output literal does not display its whole build path; users read that path through `jet inspect output`.

decisions.title: What should Jet call the complete project graph?
decisions.gist: Choose the ordinary type name for the value that connects everything one Jet project builds, runs, and deploys.
decisions.lesson:
Graph: a set of named values connected by checked references.
Root: the single top value from which Jet reaches that graph.
Binding: the lowercase variable name used for a value.
Checked: Jet verified every name, type, and connection.

The root can connect packages, environments, services, images, systems, and fleets. It describes their shared meaning without requiring one folder, repository, or file layout.

A beginner can still run a file containing only `fn run()`. Teams meet this type when one program grows into a package or deployed system. Experts use the same value for inspection and audit.

This ballot chooses only the type noun and conventional lowercase binding. Other decisions own graph scope, fields, files, composition, storage, and commands.
decisions.story: Rin's Greeter starts as one command. It gains an API package, development environment, release image, and home server. Documentation and diagnostics now need one stable noun for their connected definition.
decisions.inWild: Cargo calls a package group a workspace, but that word usually follows a checkout boundary. Terraform calls its entry configuration a root module. Nix flakes can expose packages, development shells, applications, and operating systems from one value. Jet needs an ordinary noun for a typed value that may cover all those roles.

options.name: Project
options.detail: Use `Project` and `project`. Beginners already know the word, and it can naturally own code, environments, services, images, machines, and fleets.
options.technical: Project names the complete checked value, not a directory or build invocation. Package, Environment, Service, Image, Fleet, and System keep narrower meanings.

options.name: Workspace
options.detail: Use `Workspace` and `workspace`. The name suggests related work managed together, especially in editors and monorepos.
options.technical: Workspace means a durable checked graph, not a checkout or editor session. That differs from common tool usage.

options.name: Stack
options.detail: Use `Stack` and `stack`. The word fits software, services, infrastructure, and operating-system pieces deployed together.
options.technical: Stack names the complete graph, not an ordered collection. It also appears in call-stack and data-structure diagnostics.

options.name: Graph
options.detail: Use `Graph` and `graph`. The name directly describes connected typed values and avoids implying a repository boundary.
options.technical: Jet also has narrower dependency, build, and execution graphs. Public copy must distinguish the complete Graph from those views.

options.name: Root
options.detail: Use `Root` and `root`. The word is short and describes the value from which all connected parts are reachable.
options.technical: Root describes graph position. It also means a filesystem boundary, package directory, tree node, or privileged operating-system account.

options.name: Configuration
options.detail: Use `Configuration` and `configuration`. The word makes desired state sound declarative and reviewable.
options.technical: The graph also contains executable packages, actions, realized outputs, and provenance. Configuration understates those values.

options.name: Model
options.detail: Use `Model` and `model`. The word suggests one checked description from which tools derive builds and deployments.
options.technical: Model is broad but generic. It collides with application data models, compiler models, and machine-learning models.

options.name: Platform
options.detail: Use `Platform` and `platform`. The word spans applications, shared services, tooling, infrastructure, and machines.
options.technical: Platform often means a reusable foundation rather than one complete product graph. Small projects may sound larger than they are.

options.name: Package
options.detail: Use `Package` for the complete repository-neutral semantic whole. A monorepo root lists independent member Packages by reference; a member cannot list members.
options.technical: The nearest `package.jet` defines one Package. Membership depth is capped at one. A single Package needs no `members:` field, and no second Workspace noun is introduced.
options.code: members: find("./packages")

comparisons.note: A flake exposes packages, apps, development shells, and machine configurations from one source value. Its noun requires Nix-specific teaching.
Terraform calls the top configuration a root module. Root explains graph position, while module explains composition.

recommendation.why: Package gives one noun from a small program through a fleet and fits Jetpack. Flat references keep monorepos explicit without recursive Package containment.

whyNot.reason: Project duplicates Package as a second noun for the same semantic whole.
Workspace introduces a checkout-oriented second noun and boundary.
Stack is overloaded and does not name a distribution unit.
Graph names representation instead of the user-owned unit.
Root names position and conflicts with filesystem and privilege terms.
Configuration understates executable outputs, actions, and provenance.
Model is generic and collides with application and compiler models.
Platform sounds like a reusable foundation rather than one package.

recommendation.tradeoff: Package must cover both an ordinary package and a monorepo root. The depth-one members law keeps that meaning finite.

decisions.checkInstructions: This naming remains conditional on the unified graph scope owned by D-ECO1. After ratification, replace the `<Root>` placeholder without adding aliases.

decisions.title: JetOS plan and historical proof
decisions.gist: Decide whether proof preserves the exact built delta from a captured parent generation.
decisions.lesson: `jet os plan` predicts changes from checked Package source and the active baseline before a machine changes. Build captures the parent generation. `jet os proof` records what was built and observed. Historical proof can store that exact baseline-relative delta, or omit it and leave only the current prediction path.
decisions.story: Rin changes Halcyon's API port during an incident. Before activation Rin needs a preview; later an auditor needs the exact change from gen-41 to gen-42 after newer generations are active.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's Package graph produces System Output `halcyon`. Plan predicts `gen-41 -> candidate`; proof for `gen-42` preserves baseline, built changes, output digests, readiness, activation, provenance, and rollback.

options.name: Plan predicts, proof confirms
options.detail: Plan shows the checked prediction. Proof stores the exact built delta from the captured baseline with evidence.
options.code:
$ jet os plan halcyon
Plan: halcyon
baseline: gen-41 (active)
candidate: not built

$ jet os proof halcyon --name gen-42
Proof: halcyon generation gen-42
baseline: gen-41
changes: 1 added, 1 changed, 0 removed
readiness: passed (12/12 checks)
provenance: complete

options.name: Plan is the only delta
options.detail: Plan predicts current changes, while proof stores readiness and provenance without a baseline delta.
options.code:
$ jet os plan halcyon
baseline: gen-41 (active)
  + service api

$ jet os proof halcyon --name gen-42
readiness: passed (12/12 checks)
provenance: complete
changes: not recorded

recommendation.why: Plan gives the immediate safe preview, and proof answers the later historical question after active state changes without adding another command.

whyNot.reason: A later plan compares against current state and cannot reconstruct what an older generation changed from its captured parent.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each generation retains a compact typed delta and activation observation record.

decisions.title: What should Jet call one modular graph contribution?
decisions.gist: Choose the public type name for one self-contained piece that joins other pieces into a project's complete checked graph.
decisions.lesson:
Graph: a set of named values connected by references.
Root: the top value containing the complete graph.
Contribution: one value that adds facts to that root.
Closed: the value uses only its declarations and explicit imports.
Composition: the rule that combines contributions.

A team may keep one contribution beside deployment code and another beside monitoring code. Jet checks each value alone, then combines them by one composition law.

Equal facts coalesce. Different facts at the same single-value path produce an error naming both sources.

Jet already uses module for a namespace. Reusing module here would give one word two semantic jobs.

This ballot chooses only the contribution type name. It does not choose filenames, discovery, root name, fields, split policy, or commands.
decisions.story: Mara's shop API gains deployment and monitoring files. Both set `services.api.port` differently. Jet's error must name each self-contained value without forcing Mara to decode product jargon.
decisions.inWild: NixOS users split one machine configuration into modules, which merge through Nix rules and priorities. Terraform modules package declarations behind inputs and outputs. Rust modules and Go packages organize namespaces. npm packages are distribution units. Jet cannot reuse module because that word already names its namespace mechanism. It needs a separate noun for a checked graph contribution.

options.name: Rib
options.detail: Use `Rib`. Aircraft ribs are repeated structural members that join into a larger frame.
options.technical: Rib collides with Golem's Rib programming language and Pixar RenderMan's RIB format. Anatomy and food meanings add search noise.

options.name: Wing
options.detail: Use `Wing`. The word is short, familiar, aviation-rooted, and suggests a substantial part joined to a larger craft.
options.technical: Wing collides with Winglang, a cloud programming language. An aircraft usually has few wings, while a project may have many contributions.

options.name: Bay
options.detail: Use `Bay`. An aircraft bay is a bounded place for one coherent system or payload.
options.technical: Bay has prior container and cloud uses, including OpenStack Magnum's former cluster term. Geography and storage hardware add search noise.

options.name: Section
options.detail: Use `Section`. The ordinary word is familiar and fits one coherent region of an aircraft or technical plan.
options.technical: Section is common in object files, documents, configuration formats, UI types, and cloud product names. Search precision is weak.

options.name: Cell
options.detail: Use `Cell`. The word strongly suggests a small self-contained unit that joins peers into a whole.
options.technical: Jet uses Cell internally for runtime concepts, and Rust exposes `std::cell::Cell`. Compiler discussion and searches would be ambiguous.

options.name: Nacelle
options.detail: Use `Nacelle`. A nacelle is a distinct aircraft housing integrated into a larger craft.
options.technical: Nacelle is unfamiliar to many beginners and more naturally names a housing than its contents. It also names an active commerce platform.

options.name: Config
options.detail: Use `Config` for one layout-neutral typed value that contributes Package facts.
options.technical: Config is distinct from a code module and from a distributable Package. Configs merge by the ratified field law and cannot declare member Packages.

comparisons.note: NixOS modules contribute options and configuration to one system. Jet cannot reuse module because that word already names source namespaces.
Terraform modules package resources behind inputs and outputs. Jet contributions remain ordinary typed values discovered by one root.

recommendation.why: Config is plain English and separates settings contributions from code namespaces and distribution units.

whyNot.reason: Rib is themed and collides with language and graphics names.
Wing is themed and collides with Winglang.
Bay sounds like a location rather than contributed facts.
Section is heavily overloaded and does not state configuration purpose.
Cell collides with memory and runtime vocabulary.
Nacelle requires aviation vocabulary and names a housing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Config is a common word. Type context and Package-qualified documentation must keep it distinct from ad hoc configuration files.

decisions.checkInstructions: Replace contribution placeholders only after ratification. Source discovery and split behavior remain separate decisions. Do not add aliases for rejected names.

decisions.title: What jet split does with inline Package facts
decisions.gist: Decide whether `jet split` extracts inline facts or only moves an already-authored Config.
decisions.lesson: A Config is a typed value contributing facts to one Package. `jet split` is a source refactor that must preserve Package identity and graph fingerprint. The command previews its generated binding, refuses non-closed extraction before writes, and records a ledger that `jet fold` can reverse. This decision controls whether split may create the Config a beginner has not written yet.
decisions.story: Maya starts with a development environment inline in `package.jet`. When the file grows, she asks Jet to move the environment into `package/env.jet` without first learning the manual Config extraction steps.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's S3 transition extracts `package.environments` into `package/env.jet::development`, adds a `Config`, and proves the Package graph hash is unchanged. Experts may author that same Config directly.

options.name: Extract and move
options.detail: Split creates the closed Config needed to move inline facts and records a reversible ledger.
options.code:
$ jet split env --check
Would extract: package.environments
Would create: package/env.jet::development
Would add: Config `development`
package graph before: sha256:39df…
package graph after:  sha256:39df…
No files changed.

options.name: Move Configs only
options.detail: Split moves only an exported Config the author already created. Inline facts fail with a direct prerequisite.
options.code:
$ jet split env
Error: no exported Config owns tier env.
Fix: extract it, then retry.

recommendation.why: The command fulfills the requested growth step and produces the same Config experts write directly.

whyNot.reason: It requires the common one-file growth path to perform a manual extraction before the refactor command can help.

recommendation.tradeoff: Preview must name the generated binding and split must refuse shared bindings, collisions, and open fields before any write.

decisions.checkInstructions: Preserve exact ledger, refusal, precedence, graph-fingerprint, crash-safety, and round-trip laws in technical acceptance. Substitute the type ratified by D-ECO-SLICENAME1 in executable fixtures.

decisions.title: What should manual Hangar-root actions be called?
decisions.gist: Choose one naming family for creating, removing, and listing manual roots under `jet hangar`.
decisions.lesson:
Garbage collection, or GC, is cleanup that deletes stored software Jet can prove nobody still needs.
Output: one immutable result already stored in Hangar.
Realized: already built or downloaded.
Closure: an output plus every stored dependency it needs.
Root: a durable record telling GC to keep one output and its closure.
Lease: temporary protection tied to running work, such as a build or process.
Manual root: durable protection created for software outside Jet.
Etag: a version stamp that blocks stale updates.

Jet creates roots automatically for projects, profiles, toolchains, and JetOS generations. It creates leases automatically while programs and builds run. An external backup appliance falls outside those lifecycles.

Creating a manual root never builds or downloads anything. It accepts only an output already in Hangar. Removing the root, or reaching its expiry, ends protection only when no other root or lease reaches that closure.

Ratified decisions already put physical lifecycle actions under `jet hangar` and require one noun-then-verb grouped grammar. This ballot still needs owner confirmation for the three new user-facing action names.
decisions.story: Asha's nightly backup service loads an SDK from Hangar. Its project disappears Friday. Saturday's `jet clean` must not delete the SDK before Sunday's backup, so Asha creates a named root.
decisions.inWild: Nix exposes GC roots as filesystem links. Indirect roots add another link under Nix's automatic-root directory, and operators inspect roots separately. Rust, Go, and npm caches do not durably declare that an outside service needs one complete immutable dependency closure. Jet uses one typed record with expiry and stale-update protection. This expert escape hatch exists because no project, profile, process, or build owns the appliance's SDK.

options.name: Add, remove, list external roots
options.detail: Use `add-external-root`, `remove-external-root`, and `list-external-roots`. Help and audit logs always state the stored object and operation. The names are long but immediately literal.
options.technical: This confirms only three action spellings. Existing root lifecycle, plan/apply, etag, ownership, expiry, audit, and JSON laws remain separate contract material.
options.code:
$ jet hangar help
Actions:
  add-external-root
  remove-external-root
  list-external-roots

$ jet hangar add-external-root backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --expires-in 12w --yes
Plan external root
+ backup-sdk
  closure objects: 3
  etag: 1.1
  expires: 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z
created external root 1.1

$ jet hangar add-external-root backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --if-etag 1.0 --yes
Error [E1320]: External root `principal:mzxw6ytboi2dknjvgy3tqojqge/backup-sdk` changed; expected etag `1.0`, current etag is `1.1`.
 Why: Compare-and-swap and never-reused incarnations prevent lost updates and delete-and-recreate identity reuse.
 Fix: Inspect the current root and audit, then retry with `--if-etag 1.1` only if that state is intended.
No requested root mutation was applied.

options.name: Register, unregister, list external roots
options.detail: Use `register-external-root`, `unregister-external-root`, and `list-external-roots`. Register says Jet records an existing output without building or downloading it. Unregister clearly removes only that record.
options.technical: This confirms only three action spellings. Existing root lifecycle, plan/apply, etag, ownership, expiry, audit, and JSON laws remain separate contract material.
options.code:
$ jet hangar help
Actions:
  register-external-root
  unregister-external-root
  list-external-roots

$ jet hangar register-external-root backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --expires-in 12w --yes
Plan external root
+ backup-sdk
  closure objects: 3
  etag: 1.1
  expires: 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z
created external root 1.1

$ jet hangar register-external-root backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --if-etag 1.0 --yes
Error [E1320]: External root `principal:mzxw6ytboi2dknjvgy3tqojqge/backup-sdk` changed; expected etag `1.0`, current etag is `1.1`.
 Why: Compare-and-swap and never-reused incarnations prevent lost updates and delete-and-recreate identity reuse.
 Fix: Inspect the current root and audit, then retry with `--if-etag 1.1` only if that state is intended.
No requested root mutation was applied.

options.name: Keep, release, list kept
options.detail: Use `keep`, `release`, and `list-kept`. These names are quick to type and read naturally as lifecycle actions. Help and audit logs need surrounding Hangar context to reveal root semantics.
options.technical: This confirms only three action spellings. Existing root lifecycle, plan/apply, etag, ownership, expiry, audit, and JSON laws remain separate contract material.
options.code:
$ jet hangar help
Actions:
  keep
  release
  list-kept

$ jet hangar keep backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --expires-in 12w --yes
Plan external root
+ backup-sdk
  closure objects: 3
  etag: 1.1
  expires: 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z
created external root 1.1

$ jet hangar keep backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --if-etag 1.0 --yes
Error [E1320]: External root `principal:mzxw6ytboi2dknjvgy3tqojqge/backup-sdk` changed; expected etag `1.0`, current etag is `1.1`.
 Why: Compare-and-swap and never-reused incarnations prevent lost updates and delete-and-recreate identity reuse.
 Fix: Inspect the current root and audit, then retry with `--if-etag 1.1` only if that state is intended.
No requested root mutation was applied.

options.name: Pin, unpin, list external pins
options.detail: Use `pin-external`, `unpin-external`, and `list-external-pins`. Pin is familiar cache language and makes retention intent obvious. It can be confused with package-version pinning elsewhere in Jet.
options.technical: This confirms only three action spellings. Existing root lifecycle, plan/apply, etag, ownership, expiry, audit, and JSON laws remain separate contract material.
options.code:
$ jet hangar help
Actions:
  pin-external
  unpin-external
  list-external-pins

$ jet hangar pin-external backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --expires-in 12w --yes
Plan external root
+ backup-sdk
  closure objects: 3
  etag: 1.1
  expires: 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z
created external root 1.1

$ jet hangar pin-external backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --if-etag 1.0 --yes
Error [E1320]: External root `principal:mzxw6ytboi2dknjvgy3tqojqge/backup-sdk` changed; expected etag `1.0`, current etag is `1.1`.
 Why: Compare-and-swap and never-reused incarnations prevent lost updates and delete-and-recreate identity reuse.
 Fix: Inspect the current root and audit, then retry with `--if-etag 1.1` only if that state is intended.
No requested root mutation was applied.

comparisons.note: Nix manual roots use filesystem links. Jet uses named typed records, so moving a working directory cannot silently change root identity.

recommendation.why: Register precisely describes creating durable metadata for an existing output. It scans clearly in help, distinguishes registration from realization, and makes removal scope explicit in audit logs.

whyNot.reason: Add and remove are familiar, but add can suggest importing or realizing an output instead of recording retention metadata.
Short verbs are pleasant interactively, but `keep` and `list-kept` hide root kind in help, scripts, and detached audit records.
Pin and unpin clearly imply retention, but Jet users may confuse them with package-version pins.

recommendation.tradeoff: Register and unregister are long, formal words. Manual roots are rare expert actions, and precision matters more than saving keystrokes.

decisions.checkInstructions: Ratify exactly one three-action family with no aliases. Do not infer or reopen lifecycle semantics from this naming ballot.

decisions.title: Exact Nix 2.34.8 oracle and nixpkgs source
decisions.gist: Choose the exact nixpkgs snapshot used inside Jetpack's fixed, platform-verified Nix 2.34.8 oracle boundary.
decisions.lesson:
Nix and nixpkgs are different inputs. Nix is the evaluator and build tool. nixpkgs is a repository of package definitions interpreted by that tool. Compatibility evidence must identify both, because changing either input can change derivations and store paths.

Nix 2.34.8 has an official annotated Git tag. An annotated tag is its own Git object, which points to a source commit. The tag object is `b6769c588f60b3e762f73d3a8cf60294df078ccd`. Its peeled source commit is `f3f1c3c5b8ad91850e0f7c590cf177f7ab022024`. Recording both prevents a moving tag name from changing the selected source.

Those two identifiers pin source history, not a runnable build. Compiler versions, linked libraries, build flags, and target systems can still change the produced Nix executable. A source tag alone therefore cannot prove which executable generated an oracle fixture.

A Nix Archive, called a NAR, is Nix's canonical filesystem serialization. Each supported oracle platform records one NAR hash for the built install output and one for the executable used by tests. Missing or mismatched hashes block fixture generation and acceptance. No fallback silently rebuilds a different oracle.

The remaining choice is the nixpkgs snapshot interpreted by that fixed oracle. Beginners receive no prompt or setting. Experts can inspect one manifest containing exact Nix source, exact nixpkgs source, platform build identities, fixture systems, and corpus status. Future movement requires a new decision and a green differential corpus.
decisions.story: Mara updates Jet's development shell while a macOS compatibility fixture changes. The manifest proves whether nixpkgs moved, the Nix source moved, or a platform rebuilt Nix differently. Until each platform's executable and build hashes are recorded, the test refuses to bless new output. Beginners still see the same native package workflow.

options.name: Current repository nixpkgs lock
options.detail: Use the nixpkgs snapshot already locked by Jet's current root flake. Copy its revision and NAR hash into the immutable compatibility manifest. Pair it with the exact Nix 2.34.8 tag object, peeled source commit, and required platform build hashes. Beginners receive no configuration. Experts get a nixpkgs source already used by the repository, while oracle execution remains blocked until every required build identity is populated.
options.technical: Nix is exactly version 2.34.8, annotated tag object `b6769c588f60b3e762f73d3a8cf60294df078ccd`, peeled source commit `f3f1c3c5b8ad91850e0f7c590cf177f7ab022024`. nixpkgs is revision `b5aa0fbd538984f6e3d201be0005b4463d8b09f8`, `lastModified = 1782723713`, and `narHash = sha256-oPXCU/SSUokcGaJREHibG1CBX3+s/W7orDWQOZDsEeQ=` from root `flake.lock` at repository commit `6a01b05f0acca94b2cbdd7fddd14de315234d7ab`. Each supported oracle system must record `build_nar_hash` for the complete Nix install output and `executable_nar_hash` for the exact executable invoked. Null, absent, unknown-system, or mismatched values stop generation and acceptance before any expected bytes change. The tag object and source commit never substitute for those hashes.

options.name: Original repository nixpkgs lock
options.detail: Use the nixpkgs snapshot from Jet's original root flake lock. It remains byte-identifiable in repository history. The same exact Nix 2.34.8 source and per-platform build-hash gate apply. Beginners still see nothing. Experts gain an older repository-proven nixpkgs baseline, but it no longer represents any current Jet environment. Oracle execution remains blocked until every platform build identity is populated.
options.technical: Nix is exactly version 2.34.8 with tag object `b6769c588f60b3e762f73d3a8cf60294df078ccd` and peeled commit `f3f1c3c5b8ad91850e0f7c590cf177f7ab022024`. nixpkgs is revision `a799d3e3886da994fa307f817a6bc705ae538eeb`, `lastModified = 1780749050`, and `narHash = sha256-3av0pIjlOWQ6rDbNOmpUSvbNnJkGORQKKjb4LtCZsIY=` from root `flake.lock` at repository commit `baa917d6c53a19914898f214934658bd02d76d8f`. Every supported system still needs exact build-output and executable NAR hashes. Source identifiers alone never authorize fixture generation, differential acceptance, or corpus claims.

options.name: JetOS fixture nixpkgs revision
options.detail: Use the nixpkgs commit already exercised by JetOS fixtures. The fixture lacks a nixpkgs NAR hash, so source normalization is incomplete. Exact Nix 2.34.8 source and platform build identities are also mandatory. This option remains blocked on both the nixpkgs NAR hash and every oracle build hash. Beginners remain unaffected. Experts see each missing identity instead of an inferred or locally rebuilt substitute.
options.technical: Nix is exactly version 2.34.8 with tag object `b6769c588f60b3e762f73d3a8cf60294df078ccd` and peeled commit `f3f1c3c5b8ad91850e0f7c590cf177f7ab022024`. nixpkgs commit is `fef9403a3e4d31b0a23f0bacebbec52c248fbb51`. Local evidence appears in `tests/support/jetpack_fixtures.rs`, `tests/jetpack_jetos.rs`, and `tests/fixtures/jetpack-config-real/config.jet`. Those synthetic locks omit nixpkgs `narHash`. The compatibility manifest must populate that hash plus each platform's Nix build-output and executable NAR hashes. No source tag, local `nix` binary, or successful evaluation weakens the fail-closed gate.

comparisons.note: An annotated tag is a Git object that points to another object. Recording the tag object and peeled commit fixes the selected source relationship. It says nothing about compiler inputs or produced executable bytes.
A flake lock pairs a source revision with a NAR hash for normalized source. Jet's oracle adds platform build-output and executable hashes because identical source can still produce different tools.
comparisons.code: source revision + source NAR hash + platform build NAR hash + executable NAR hash

comparisons.note: A compiler source commit and a distributed compiler binary are separate identities. Reproducible testing records both. Jet applies the same rule to Nix source and each oracle executable.
comparisons.code: rust source commit != rustc artifact hash

recommendation.why: It combines the fixed Nix 2.34.8 source boundary with the only nixpkgs candidate that has a complete source identity and a current repository role. Platform build hashes remain mandatory, so present repository use cannot masquerade as oracle proof. Beginners stay ceremony-free; experts receive exact source, build, executable, platform, and corpus facts.

whyNot.reason: Its nixpkgs source identity is complete, but the snapshot no longer anchors a current repository environment. It adds no stronger evaluator or build guarantee than the recommended source.
Its migration coverage is useful, but the nixpkgs NAR hash is missing. It begins with one more unresolved identity while retaining the same platform build requirements.

recommendation.tradeoff: The chosen nixpkgs snapshot was selected for Jet's development environment, not specifically for evaluator coverage. Corpus rows remain separately reviewed, and no row runs until exact Nix build identities exist.

decisions.checkInstructions: After ratification, commit `tests/fixtures/nix-compat/oracle.json` with Nix version 2.34.8, annotated tag object `b6769c588f60b3e762f73d3a8cf60294df078ccd`, peeled source commit `f3f1c3c5b8ad91850e0f7c590cf177f7ab022024`, selected nixpkgs revision, and nixpkgs NAR hash. Record each supported oracle system explicitly. For every system, build through one declared recipe and record the complete install-output NAR hash plus the exact invoked executable NAR hash. Null, absent, unknown-system, or mismatched hashes must fail before fixture generation, snapshot update, expected-byte acceptance, or parity claims. Prove a tag-name match, tag-object match, or source-commit match alone cannot pass the build gate. Prove ordinary root `flake.lock` updates cannot mutate the oracle manifest. Differential CI must verify the executable hash before invocation and the build hash before accepting results. A future Nix source, build recipe, platform build, or nixpkgs re-pin requires a green proposed corpus and a new owner amendment. If C wins, its nixpkgs NAR hash must also be populated before any corpus row can run.

decisions.title: Safe authority for dev-service trees
decisions.gist: Choose whether safe background dev services activate per platform or wait until every supported platform has complete-tree authority.
decisions.lesson:
A process identifier, usually called a PID, is a reusable number. A start time detects common reuse, but it cannot bind a later signal to the process that was checked.

A service is a changing process tree. A child can create a new session with `setsid`, leave its parent's process group, and keep running after a parent-only shutdown.

Safe shutdown needs an operating system authority that owns the complete tree. Linux systemd user units can own a delegated control group. Windows Job Objects can contain a suspended child before user code runs.

macOS launchd can identify its registered job, but ordinary launchd control cannot contain a hostile descendant after `setsid`. A random label avoids PID reuse for the main job, not escaped-tree survival.

Startup must also survive crashes without guessing. `Pending` means user code is blocked. `Ready` means containment is proved and release is authorized. `Stopping` forbids replacement until the exact authority is empty.

Every state replacement and containing directory is synced before the next step. An old generation cannot be replaced until its authority is empty and its state removal is durable.

This decision adds no Jet syntax, manifest field, command, or flag. Existing service commands work automatically where policy permits. Unsupported authority returns E1332 before user code starts.

The narrow no-daemon amendment permits only per-service lifetime authority. It allows an existing user system manager and a Windows guardian while that declared service runs. Root, package background work, and a global Jetpack daemon remain forbidden.
decisions.story: Mira starts a database, then stops it after the original shell PID has been reused. A plugin creates a new session. Jetpack must stop only the original tree. If startup crashes halfway, the next command must resume one durable transition instead of trusting a PID file.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet services up
web: starting
web: healthy

$ jet services health --json
{"service":"web","state":"healthy","authority":{"version":2,"generation":"7cb8…","phase":"Ready","backend":"systemd-user-cgroup","containment":"complete-tree"}}

$ jet services down
web: stopped

When policy cannot activate safe background authority:

$ jet services up
Error [E1332]: Safe service authority is unavailable for `web`.
 Why: Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.
 Fix: Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.
No service command was started. No process was signaled.

options.name: Activate each proved platform
options.detail: Enable background services where complete-tree authority is proved. Linux uses a transient systemd user unit with a delegated control group. Windows uses a project-local guardian and Job Object. macOS fails before spawn. Existing commands remain ceremony-free. Structured output exposes backend, generation, phase, containment, and recovery facts.
options.technical: This narrowly amends D-JPK-NODAEMON1. A declared service may use an existing user system manager or one per-service Windows guardian only during that service's lifetime. Root, a global Jetpack daemon, package background work, new syntax, new manifest fields, and new CLI remain forbidden. D-JPK-PLATFORM1 is narrowed only for macOS background service containment. E1332 has one exact copy. What: `Safe service authority is unavailable for {name}.` Why: `Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.` Fix: `Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.` Linux creates a random transient user unit whose wrapper blocks on a generation gate. Jetpack proves manager authority, unit identity, delegated control group, and complete-tree containment before Ready. Missing authority returns E1332 before release. Stop targets the unit and control group, never a PID. systemd remains owner after Jetpack exits; Jetpack never claims its own loss kills that tree. Windows creates the child suspended. A guardian creates the sole non-inheritable Job handle, denies breakaway, enables KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, assigns the child, and acknowledges containment. Jetpack publishes durable Ready before requesting resume. Guardian loss closes the last Job handle and kills the contained tree. Down authenticates the random-generation endpoint and terminates the Job. macOS returns E1332 before spawn. Start writes and syncs Pending with generation and backend, spawns blocked, proves containment, atomically publishes and syncs Ready, then sends an idempotent release. Pending recovery stops provisional authority, proves it empty, removes state, and syncs the directory. Ready recovery retries release when acknowledgement is absent. Explicit release rejection first publishes durable Stopping. Down publishes and syncs Stopping before termination. Stopping recovery repeats exact-authority shutdown until empty, then removes state and syncs the directory. Old generation replacement cannot start before old authority emptiness and durable state removal. Spawn or containment failure removes Pending only after proving no child ran or provisional authority is empty. Ready publication failure stops containment and retains Pending when cleanup is uncertain. Ambiguous release retains Ready for idempotent recovery. No path signals from PID, start time, process name, or legacy record.
options.code:
$ jet services up
cache: starting
cache: healthy

# Crash after Ready sync, before release acknowledgement:
$ jet services up
cache: recovering Ready generation 7cb8…
cache: healthy

$ jet services down
cache: stopped

# macOS, or missing proved authority:
$ jet services up
Error [E1332]: Safe service authority is unavailable for `web`.
 Why: Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.
 Fix: Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.
No service command was started. No process was signaled.

options.name: Wait for universal authority
options.detail: Disable background services on every supported platform until all platforms provide atomic complete-tree authority. Every host returns E1332 before spawn. Linux and Windows backends remain inactive despite their proofs. This preserves one universal availability boundary and the same safety contract. Existing service declarations remain captured but cannot run in background mode.
options.technical: No backend activates until Linux, Windows, and macOS all pass the same native authority contract. D-JPK-NODAEMON1 remains unchanged while background mode is disabled. When the universal gate opens, it receives only the same per-service lifetime amendment described by Option A. E1332 uses the same exact copy on every host. What: `Safe service authority is unavailable for {name}.` Why: `Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.` Fix: `Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.` No unsafe override or cooperative exception exists. `jet dev` stops before user code when a declared service cannot start. Activation still requires the complete transaction. Start writes and syncs Pending with generation and backend, spawns blocked, proves containment, atomically publishes and syncs Ready, then sends an idempotent release. Pending recovery stops provisional authority, proves it empty, removes state, and syncs the directory. Ready recovery retries release when acknowledgement is absent. Explicit release rejection first publishes durable Stopping. Down publishes and syncs Stopping before termination. Stopping recovery repeats exact-authority shutdown until empty, then removes state and syncs the directory. Old generation replacement cannot start before old authority emptiness and durable state removal. Spawn or containment failure removes Pending only after proving no child ran or provisional authority is empty. Ready publication failure stops containment and retains Pending when cleanup is uncertain. Ambiguous release retains Ready for idempotent recovery. No path signals from PID, start time, process name, or legacy record.
options.code:
$ jet services up
Error [E1332]: Safe service authority is unavailable for `web`.
 Why: Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.
 Fix: Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.
No service command was started. No process was signaled.

comparisons.note: A transient user unit owns a control group. Control-group shutdown reaches descendants after new sessions, while unit authority survives the Jetpack command that created it.
A suspended child cannot escape before Job assignment. Denied breakaway contains descendants. A sole guardian handle makes guardian loss terminate the Job tree.
A launchd label avoids PID reuse for the registered job. It does not prove containment of a descendant after that descendant creates a new session.
comparisons.code: launchd label authority != hostile descendant containment

recommendation.why: It spends availability only where complete-tree authority is absent. Linux and Windows keep ceremony-free safe services. macOS refuses before user code starts. Experts receive exact lifecycle and containment evidence without a hidden fallback.

whyNot.reason: It is safe, but disables already-proved Linux and Windows authority. Waiting for macOS adds no stronger containment to those hosts and removes a useful safe default.

recommendation.tradeoff: Background dev services remain unavailable on macOS until complete-tree authority exists. A loud pre-start refusal is accepted because false shutdown success would violate the service safety contract.

decisions.checkInstructions: Reserve genuinely free E1332 with exactly this diagnostic. What: `Safe service authority is unavailable for {name}.` Why: `Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.` Fix: `Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.` Add this exact what, why, and fix to `docs/spec/diagnostics.md`. Add UI and CLI snapshots before shipment; I4 forbids claiming the diagnostic exists without both registry and snapshot coverage. Add no Jet syntax, manifest field, CLI command, or flag. If A wins, amend D-JPK-NODAEMON1 only for declared-service lifetime authority. Permit an existing user system manager and one per-service Windows guardian while that service runs. Continue forbidding root, global daemons, and package background work. Narrow D-JPK-PLATFORM1 only for macOS background containment. Prove every Pending write, directory sync, blocked spawn, containment proof, Ready replacement, Ready sync, release, Stopping replacement, Stopping sync, termination, emptiness proof, state removal, and final directory sync failpoint. Prove old-generation replacement cannot begin before old authority is empty and old state removal is durable. Force PID reuse between every probe and stop; unrelated processes must survive. Spawn descendants that call `setsid` during graceful and forced shutdown. Linux passes only when the transient user unit and delegated control group remain authoritative and empty after stop. Never claim Jetpack loss kills a Linux control group. Windows passes only with create-suspended ordering, sole non-inheritable Job authority, no breakaway, KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, guardian-loss tree kill, and resume after durable Ready. Under A, macOS must return E1332 before spawning user code. Under B, every host must return the identical E1332 copy before spawning user code. Prove legacy PID-only and PID/start records are quarantined without signaling. Native Linux, Windows, and macOS CI must execute real platform paths; source-token tests cannot substitute.

decisions.title: How Packages relate in a monorepo
decisions.gist: Decide whether a monorepo Package refers to independent member Packages or contains recursive Package definitions.
decisions.lesson: A Package is the complete checked unit defined by its nearest `package.jet`. A member reference points from a monorepo root to another Package. Depth cap 1 means a member Package cannot list members. This decision controls only Package membership. Config composition, source imports, and repository layout remain separate.
decisions.story: Mara keeps an API and billing tool in one repository. The root must name both without letting billing define another hidden Package tree that changes discovery and lock identity.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's enterprise monorepo uses one root `members:` list. A nested member is rejected with a diagnostic naming both `package.jet` files and telling the user to lift the inner references.

options.name: Flat member references
options.detail: The root lists member Packages by reference. Members cannot have members, and a single Package needs no membership field.
options.code:
members: find("./packages")

$ jet check
Error: member package `packages/api/package.jet` lists members from `packages/api/modules/package.jet`
 What: root `package.jet` references `packages/api/package.jet`, which also has a `members:` field
 Why: package membership has depth cap 1; members cannot have members
 Fix: remove the inner `members:` field and lift its references into root `package.jet`

options.name: Recursive Packages
options.detail: Every Package may contain more Packages through `members:`. Discovery and lock identity follow the full tree.

options.name: Workspace root plus Packages
options.detail: A separate Workspace type owns Package membership. Individual Packages never have `members:`.

options.name: Named sub-units
options.detail: The root contains differently named sub-units instead of member Packages.

recommendation.why: Flat references keep one Package noun, one membership boundary, and one deterministic depth rule while supporting monorepos.

whyNot.reason: Recursive membership makes discovery, identity, and diagnostics depend on an unbounded Package tree.
A Workspace type restores the second root noun the Package choice removed.
A renamed sub-unit creates another distribution concept beside Package.

recommendation.tradeoff: Large monorepos must list every member from the root instead of grouping them through nested Package membership.

decisions.title: Commands for Package growth and reversal
decisions.gist: Choose the commands that extract Package facts and reverse a recorded extraction.
decisions.lesson: A split moves or extracts facts without changing the checked Package graph. A fold reverses a split through Jet's private provenance ledger. Both commands preview before writing, refuse unsafe boundaries, and preserve the graph fingerprint. This decision names the two commands; D-ECO-SPLITPOLICY1 separately decides whether split may create a Config from inline facts.
decisions.story: Maya's development environment outgrows `package.jet`. She extracts it, reviews the new Config, then restores the original file after a teammate asks for the earlier layout.
decisions.inWild: The proposal uses the same verbs for extracting an environment, a flat member Package, and a System-to-Fleet host map. Reversal always names the generated member file and consumes the recorded split ledger.

options.name: jet split and jet fold
options.detail: Use one extraction verb and one explicit reversal verb for every supported Package tier.
options.code:
$ jet split env
Created package/env.jet.
package graph unchanged: sha256:39df…
Reverse with: jet fold package/env.jet

options.name: jet split with reverse flag
options.detail: Use `jet split` for extraction and `jet split --reverse` for reversal.
options.code:
$ jet split env
Created package/env.jet.

$ jet split --reverse package/env.jet
Restored package.jet.

options.name: Intent-specific verbs
options.detail: Use different verbs for environments, member Packages, and Fleets.
options.code:
$ jet extract-env
$ jet extract-package billing
$ jet make-fleet halcyon
$ jet restore package/env.jet

recommendation.why: One split/fold pair applies to every graph-preserving extraction and keeps reversal visible as its own operation.

whyNot.reason: A reverse flag hides a distinct destructive direction behind the extraction command.
Tier-specific verbs create several mechanisms for the same graph-preserving refactor.

recommendation.tradeoff: Users must learn that fold is source-layout reversal, not graph aggregation or runtime behavior.

decisions.title: Fleet rollout command
decisions.gist: Choose the command for planning, staging, observing, and rolling back a Fleet rollout.
decisions.lesson: A Fleet maps host names to System Outputs plus rollout policy. Deployment builds and verifies generations, activates hosts by cohort, observes health, and rolls back according to that policy. This decision names the top-level intent. It does not change the Fleet schema or per-host activation proof.
decisions.story: Rin rolls a production Fleet through one canary and one later host. The command must read clearly in an interactive prompt, CI, and audit logs.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's beginner path runs `jet deploy prod`. Expert flags stage without activation, choose a cohort, set concurrency, emit JSON, or roll back one host without changing Fleet declarations.

options.name: jet deploy
options.detail: Use the standard deployment verb at the top level.
options.code:
$ jet deploy prod
Plan fleet `prod`
  hosts: web1, web2
  canary: web1
  then: web2
  failure: rollback changed host and stop
Push this plan? [y/N]

options.name: jet fleet push
options.detail: Group Fleet operations under a fleet noun and use push for rollout.
options.code:
$ jet fleet push prod
Plan fleet `prod`
Push this plan? [y/N]

options.name: jet os push
options.detail: Keep rollout under the JetOS command group.
options.code:
$ jet os push prod
Plan fleet `prod`
Push this plan? [y/N]

options.name: jet push
options.detail: Use the shortest top-level verb.
options.code:
$ jet push prod
Plan fleet `prod`
Push this plan? [y/N]

recommendation.why: Deploy is the established word for staged rollout and leaves push available for transfer operations.

whyNot.reason: Fleet grouping adds a noun before the primary user intent and keeps the ambiguous push verb.
OS grouping hides that one deployment spans Fleet policy, packages, services, and remote targets.
Bare push does not state whether Jet transfers source, artifacts, or activates hosts.

recommendation.tradeoff: Deploy becomes a top-level Jet command and must route to Fleet rollout without conflicting with package publication.

decisions.title: Reserved Package source-file law
decisions.gist: Decide whether one reserved `package.jet` replaces permanent package, environment, workspace, and OS role files.
decisions.lesson: A script remains complete without any reserved file. When a Package root exists, its reserved filename can supply the expected `Package` type so top-level fields construct it directly. This bare-fields root and inferred construction reuse already-ratified D-DOTCTOR2; they do not create another constructor syntax. Configs may move to discovered `.jet` files, and a leading underscore disables a discovered file. Generated state remains under `.jet/`.
decisions.story: Maya grows a script into a Package, then adds an environment and a System. She needs one place to find the Package root without learning four permanent authority files.
decisions.inWild: The proposal replaces `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `workspace.jet`, and JetOS `config.jet`. During one migration epoch, `jet init --check` previews a reversible fold and `jet init --restore-role-files` restores byte-identical originals.

options.name: One package.jet
options.detail: Use `package.jet` as the sole reserved ecosystem file. Other `.jet` files contribute Configs.
options.code:
// package.jet
systems: .{ halcyon: .System.{ packages: [cli] } }

$ jet os plan halcyon
Plan: halcyon
No machine changed.

$ jet check
Warning [L1320]: this Package uses four retired ecosystem filenames
 What: `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `workspace.jet`, and `config.jet` describe one Package
 Why: `package.jet` is now the one reserved ecosystem source file
 Fix: run `jet init --check`, review the fold, then run `jet init`

options.name: Keep role files
options.detail: Keep `pkg.jet`, `env.jet`, `workspace.jet`, and `config.jet` as permanent authorities.
options.code:
pkg.jet
env.jet
workspace.jet
config.jet

$ jet explain services.db.port
services.db.port = 5432
winning role file: env.jet

options.name: No reserved file
options.detail: Require users to select an arbitrary Package root file when one cannot be inferred.
options.code:
$ jet --package config/root.jet build
Built Package.

$ jet build
No Package root selected.

recommendation.why: One root file makes later file growth organizational, removes competing identities, and leaves the single-file script path ceremony-free.

whyNot.reason: Permanent role files preserve several authorities and require provenance to explain which file identity won.
The first multi-file Package adds permanent root-selection ceremony to normal commands.

recommendation.tradeoff: One migration epoch must teach and reversibly fold four previously ratified filenames.

decisions.title: Closed v1 Output kind set
decisions.gist: Decide whether v1 has one closed Output kind set spanning packages and JetOS results.
decisions.lesson: An Output is a named typed projection from one Package graph. A closed kind set lets selection, inspection, proof, defaults, and lifecycle commands check every case. The proposed kinds are Library, Executable, Service, Check, Environment, Image, Bundle, System, and Fleet. Adding another kind would require a later owner decision.
decisions.story: Maya's Package produces a library, command, release check, image, System, and Fleet. Tooling must know which outputs are runnable, testable, enterable, deployable, and publishable without interpreting plugin strings.
decisions.inWild: The proposal declares all nine kinds beside each other and rejects `.Wheel.{}` with a diagnostic pointing to Bundle or a future ratified kind.

options.name: Nine closed kinds
options.detail: Use Library, Executable, Service, Check, Environment, Image, Bundle, System, and Fleet as the closed v1 set.

options.name: Package-only closure
options.detail: Keep package result kinds closed while System and Fleet use separate root node types.

options.name: Extensible text kinds
options.detail: Allow plugins to introduce arbitrary Output kind strings and payloads.

recommendation.why: One closed capability model makes build, selection, inspection, proof, and defaults exhaustive from Package through Fleet.

whyNot.reason: System and Fleet would split selection, inspection, and lifecycle rules from the Output model.
Arbitrary strings prevent exhaustive tools and precise beginner diagnostics.

recommendation.tradeoff: A genuinely new output kind requires an owner decision instead of a local plugin string.

decisions.title: Storage location for connected receipts
decisions.gist: Choose where action and activation evidence lives without creating a second merge authority.
decisions.lesson: `.jet/lock` is the reviewable Package graph index and sole merge-history authority. A receipt connects locked input, action, output digest, parent generation, readiness, activation observation, and rollback evidence. Receipt storage must preserve immutable identity, retention, export, and signatures without copying graph merge history.
decisions.story: Rin builds `todo.cli` and activates Halcyon generation 42 several times while the Package source stays unchanged. The lock must remain reviewable while each realization keeps durable evidence.
decisions.inWild: The proposal stores immutable receipt objects in Hangar and records their digests in the lock or generation. `jet os proof` loads the receipt and follows its locked-input reference.

options.name: Hangar objects referenced by lock or generation
options.detail: Store receipts as immutable Hangar objects and keep only digest references in graph and generation records.
options.code:
.jet/lock contains `receipt sha256:91b8…`
$ jet os proof halcyon --name gen-42
receipt: sha256:91b8…
locked inputs: sha256:20f1…
Export copies the receipt closure.

options.name: Inline every receipt in .jet/lock
options.detail: Append action, log, output, readiness, and activation evidence directly to the Package lock.
options.code:
.jet/lock
  build todo.cli action: ...
  build todo.cli logs: ...
  system gen-42 readiness: ...
  system gen-42 activation: ...

options.name: Package-local receipt directory
options.detail: Store mutable-path JSON receipt files beside generated Package state.
options.code:
.jet/receipts/gen-42.json
$ jet os proof halcyon --name gen-42
loaded .jet/receipts/gen-42.json

recommendation.why: Hangar already owns content identity, deduplication, signatures, retention, export, and generation roots while the lock remains the one graph index.

whyNot.reason: Local realization logs and observations would grow source resolution state and obscure reviewable merge changes.
Mutable paths require another identity and tamper model for evidence already suited to content-addressed storage.

recommendation.tradeoff: Human review uses `jet proof`, `jet inspect`, or an exported receipt rather than opening one source-adjacent receipt file.

decisions.title: Default Hangar ownership and path
decisions.gist: Choose the default physical Hangar ownership model across Linux, macOS, and Windows.
decisions.lesson: Hangar stores verified immutable objects, closures, and receipts. The default path determines whether first use needs administrator setup and whether objects can be shared across a user's Packages. Shared organization storage remains a separate optional broker decision.
decisions.story: Asha installs Jet without administrator rights and runs her first Package on Linux, macOS, and Windows. The same workflow must work without a setup prompt.
decisions.inWild: The proposal uses each platform's native per-user data location and exposes the resolved value through `jet hangar path`. `/etc/jet/hangar` stops being the default.

options.name: Native per-user data path
options.detail: Use platform user-data directories and allow an optional shared broker.
options.code:
Linux:  $XDG_DATA_HOME/jet/hangar, fallback ~/.local/share/jet/hangar
macOS:  ~/Library/Application Support/Jet/Hangar
Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Jet\Hangar

$ jet hangar path
/home/asha/.local/share/jet/hangar

options.name: /etc/jet/hangar where possible
options.detail: Keep a root-owned shared path as the default on systems that provide it.
options.code:
$ jet run
permission denied: /etc/jet/hangar
rerun installer as root or configure a store

options.name: Package-local .jet/hangar
options.detail: Store objects inside each Package's generated state directory.
options.code:
weather/.jet/hangar/sha256-...
todo/.jet/hangar/sha256-...
# identical object stored once per Package

recommendation.why: Per-user storage gives rootless first use, native cross-platform behavior, and sharing across one user's Packages.

whyNot.reason: A root-owned default breaks first use without administrator setup and has no native Windows equivalent.
Package-local stores duplicate verified bytes and prevent user-wide cleanup and reuse.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each user initially owns a separate physical cache unless an administrator installs the optional shared broker.

decisions.title: Optional shared Hangar broker boundary
decisions.gist: State the privilege and lifetime boundary that keeps a shared Hangar optional and non-resident.
decisions.lesson: Jet's no-daemon rule prohibits a required resident privileged build service. An optional shared Hangar still needs a narrow authority that can verify and promote objects across users. A socket-activated process can start per request, exit when idle, refuse source evaluation, rebuild under ephemeral sandbox identities, and re-check bytes, signatures, provenance, and writer authority.
decisions.story: An administrator wants deduplicated verified objects across a build lab. Developers must still build with their own Hangars when the shared socket is absent, and the privileged component must never execute repository source.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's installer creates an optional socket. A build reports verified promotions, then the broker exits idle. Missing socket falls back to the per-user Hangar without changing Package behavior.

options.name: Socket-activated transient verifier
options.detail: Install an administrator-controlled request-bounded verifier that never evaluates source.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install
Installed socket-activated shared-store verifier.

$ jet build
shared broker verified 3 objects; broker idle exit.

# missing socket
using user Hangar

options.name: Resident build daemon
options.detail: Run a root service continuously and submit source evaluation and builds to it.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install
Enabled root build daemon.
$ jet build
submitted Package source to resident daemon

options.name: No privileged process ever
options.detail: Forbid all shared-store promotion and keep every Hangar per user.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install
unsupported

recommendation.why: Request-bounded lifetime, independent verification, ephemeral builders, and no source evaluation preserve the no-daemon promise while enabling explicit shared storage.

whyNot.reason: A resident privileged build service overturns the no-daemon and source-evaluation boundary.
A complete ban removes the already-ratified narrow path for secure cross-user promotion and canonical Nix projection.

recommendation.tradeoff: Administrators who opt in must maintain the broker socket and promotion policy.

decisions.title: Default build profile for everyday commands
decisions.gist: Which build profile the everyday commands (jet run, jet dev, jet build) use by default.
decisions.lesson:
Today the unnamed Default profile optimizes: opt-level 2, thin-LTO, and strip (Source/main.rs). Every `jet run`, `jet dev`, and `jet build` pays optimizer time, even a first hello-world run.

R8 says the default leans toward speed, but that speed is the runtime binary's, not the compile. In the edit-run loop, compile time is the speed a beginner actually feels.

D-BUILDPROFILE1 stays intact: profiles are still selected by explicit flag, never ambient env. This ballot only changes what the unnamed Default profile contains; `--release` remains the optimized profile.
decisions.story: Sam is learning Jet and runs `jet run hello.jet` after almost every edit. Each run waits on the optimizer before printing one line, so the loop feels sluggish from the first program.

options.name: Fast-codegen default, optimize behind --release
options.detail: The unnamed Default profile becomes opt-level 0, codegen-units 256, no LTO. `--release` selects the optimized, thin-LTO, stripped profile that is the default today.
options.code:
# Today (optimized default): the edit-run loop pays the optimizer each time
$ jet run hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~450 ms   (illustrative)

# Option A: opt-level 0, codegen-units 256, no LTO
$ jet run hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~150 ms   (illustrative)

# Shipping build — one flag, fully optimized + thin-LTO + strip
$ jet build --release hello.jet
$ ./hello              # same fast binary today's default produced

options.name: Split by command: run/dev fast, build optimized
options.detail: `jet run` and `jet dev` compile at opt-level 0; `jet build` keeps the optimized profile. An explicit `--profile`/`--release` flag overrides either command's default.
options.code:
# Option B: the command decides the profile
$ jet run hello.jet    # fast: opt-level 0         ~150 ms (illustrative)
$ jet dev  hello.jet   # fast: opt-level 0         ~150 ms (illustrative)
$ jet build hello.jet  # optimized: -O + thin-LTO  ~450 ms (illustrative)

# Override either way with an explicit profile flag
$ jet build --profile=debug hello.jet   # fast build of a build artifact
$ jet run   --release       hello.jet   # optimized one-off run

options.name: Keep optimized-everywhere default (status quo)
options.detail: Every everyday command keeps opt-level 2, thin-LTO, and strip. Fast compiles stay opt-in behind `--profile=debug`.
options.code:
# Option C: every everyday command optimizes (today's behavior)
$ jet run hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~450 ms   (illustrative)
$ jet build hello.jet
$ ./hello              # ~450 ms build; fast small binary

# Fast compile only if you remember the opt-in flag
$ jet run --profile=debug hello.jet
Hello, world!          # ~150 ms   (illustrative)

comparisons.note: `cargo build` is unoptimized debug by default; `cargo build --release` opts into optimization. Jet's Default profile is the opposite today, optimizing on every build.
comparisons.code:
cargo build            # debug, fast compile
cargo build --release  # optimized

comparisons.note: `zig build` produces a Debug binary by default; `-Doptimize=ReleaseFast` is the opt-in. Fast iterate, explicit ship.
`go build` has no user-picked optimize/debug split. It is fast by default, with no separate optimized build command in the everyday loop.

recommendation.why: A makes the loop beginners run hundreds of times a day instant, and keeps the optimized binary one keystroke away as `--release`.

whyNot.reason: Two profiles by command means `jet run` and `jet build` of one file can produce different binaries, so a bug seen under one may vanish under the other.
The common path stays slow: every first `jet run` pays optimizer time the beginner never asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A default binaries run slower than today's until `--release`. Everyday commands exist for iterating, not shipping, so compile speed is the right default there.

decisions.title: Backend for the explicit fast AOT debug profile
decisions.gist: D-BUILD-DEFAULT1=B already guarantees `jet build --profile=debug` as a fast on-disk AOT artifact. Choose whether rustc or Cranelift emits that existing profile; this does not add a third lens or change any command default.
decisions.lesson: Jet has one compiler core and two feature-identical lenses. The JIT lens runs `jet run` and `jet dev` quickly. The AOT lens emits binaries: `jet build` is optimized by default, while the ratified `jet build --profile=debug` asks for a fast unoptimized artifact. A profile controls optimization intent inside the AOT lens; it is not another feature tier. This ballot chooses only the debug-profile backend. Both choices consume the same sema-approved executable TIR, preserve every feature, and face R12 differential tests.
decisions.explainer: The current transpile path sends even debug-profile output through generated Rust and rustc at opt-level 0. Cranelift already serves the JIT lens and can also emit native objects on supported targets. Using it for debug-profile AOT avoids rustc re-parsing and re-verifying proven TIR, but requires native object/link/debug-info parity and a truthful target fallback. Keeping rustc is the smaller backend set but retains that redundant work. `jet run`, `jet dev`, plain `jet build`, `--profile=debug`, and `--release` keep their ratified meanings whichever backend wins.
decisions.story: Priya uses the JIT loop while editing. CI then needs a real unoptimized binary to run packaging, debugger, and deploy-shape smoke tests, so it invokes the existing debug profile. Priya wants the artifact quickly, with the same behavior and diagnostics as the optimized build, and an audit that names the backend used.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev app.jet                     # JIT lens
$ jet build app.jet                   # optimized AOT
$ jet build --profile=debug app.jet   # fast AOT artifact; this ballot chooses its backend
$ jet run --release app.jet           # explicit optimized override

$ jet explain build app.jet
profile   debug
lens      AOT
backend   cranelift | rustc-opt0
parity    executable TIR / R12
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: ordinary run/dev/build defaults stay unchanged; no backend choice is required. Expert pass: the explicit profile selects optimization intent, and build explain/audit output names backend, target support, fallback reason, timings, cache identity, and parity evidence. Backend availability may affect latency, never supported features or program behavior.

options.name: rustc opt-level 0 emits fast AOT
options.detail: Keep Cranelift JIT-only. `jet build --profile=debug` uses the current generated-Rust path with rustc optimization disabled. One native AOT backend covers every target and debug-info path, but rustc still parses and verifies code the Jet front end already proved.
options.code:
$ jet build --profile=debug app.jet
# checked Jet -> executable TIR -> generated Rust -> rustc opt-level 0 -> app
$ jet explain build app.jet
lens AOT; profile debug; backend rustc-opt0

options.name: Cranelift emits fast AOT
options.detail: Recommended. On supported targets, lower the same executable TIR through Cranelift to object code and link the debug-profile binary without generated Rust/rustc. Unsupported targets fall back to rustc opt-level 0 and report that fact; they do not lose features or silently switch optimization intent. Optimized AOT remains the existing ship backend.
options.code:
$ jet build --profile=debug app.jet
# checked Jet -> executable TIR -> Cranelift object -> app
$ jet explain build app.jet
lens AOT; profile debug; backend cranelift
# unsupported target: backend rustc-opt0; reason shown

comparisons.note: Rust uses Cranelift for faster debug codegen while LLVM remains the optimized release backend. Option B applies that backend split inside Jet's single AOT lens and existing debug/release profiles.
comparisons.code:
cargo +nightly cg_clif build   # debug
cargo build --release          # LLVM

comparisons.note: Zig uses a fast native backend for debug artifacts and an optimizing backend for release. The artifact purpose stays explicit; backend choice does not create a second language.

Go owns direct object emission, so a real binary does not require a second compiler to re-check source. Option B gives Jet's explicit debug artifact that property while retaining optimized AOT for shipping.

recommendation.why: B spends the existing Cranelift investment on the one fast on-disk artifact D-BUILD-DEFAULT1 already guarantees. It removes redundant rustc work where optimization is intentionally disabled while preserving one front end, one executable TIR, two lenses, and full feature parity.

whyNot.reason: A is sound and universal, but every debug artifact still pays generated-Rust parsing and rustc verification after Jet sema has already proved the program.

recommendation.tradeoff: B adds object/link/debug-info conformance work and per-target support accounting. Unsupported targets use the truthful rustc-opt0 fallback until their Cranelift object path passes the same R12 and native evidence gates.

decisions.comment: Owner question q4mspet2 answered with measured numbers: jet check 0.007s vs ~12s rustc path; Cranelift debug AOT lands at about check-plus-link time. His universality point about option A is preserved: B falls back to A's exact rustc-opt0 path on unsupported targets and names the fallback in jet explain build.

decisions.title: Epoch boundary for package sandbox proof
decisions.gist: Decide whether real Linux, macOS, and Windows package sandbox proof remains an Epoch 4 exit requirement or moves with JP3 to Epoch 8.
decisions.lesson:
A build sandbox is an operating-system boundary around package recipes. It limits files, processes, devices, and network access even when a recipe is hostile. A policy record saying ‘sandboxed’ is not proof; the child process must actually enter the boundary.

Epoch 4’s package-manager plan currently requires that proof before Jetpack claims full Nix replacement parity. On July 12, JP3 moved to Epoch 8 so Epoch 4 could finish package behavior first. Several live Epoch 4 cards still depend on JP3, so the board now contains two incompatible exit laws.
