Rust uses a type-owned trait method, similar to option C.

recommendation.why: It obeys the plain-word law, keeps both real jobs, and preserves the shipped Secret API. The byte qualifier makes the distinct fixed signature visible.

whyNot.reason: Public protocol bytes are not always secrets. Wrapping them adds ownership and zeroization ceremony only to reach an operation Jet already has.
It reopens the shipped Secret API and adds a cryptographic method to ordinary byte lists. The naming fix does not need that wider surface change.

recommendation.tradeoff: The byte function name is longer and repeats a type fact visible in its arguments. That cost keeps the two safe operations distinct and discoverable.

decisions.title: How can a local Jet report be shared?
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet sends report bundles, and under which privacy contract.
decisions.lesson:
A report bundle is a small local directory that helps diagnose the toolchain. Jet now creates it only when a person runs `jet report`. The person can open both text files before sharing anything. The bundle excludes source, paths, arguments, environment values, hostnames, user names, machine identifiers, network addresses, crash data, and package names.

Sharing adds a separate trust decision. A destination is where the bundle goes. A transport is how bytes reach it, usually an encrypted Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure connection. Authentication proves which person or service is allowed to send. Retention says how long the receiver keeps the report. These rules must be fixed before a command may send anything.

Even a minimal upload reveals facts outside the bundle. A server normally sees the sender's Internet Protocol address and request time. An authenticated service also learns the account identity. A public issue may keep the report indefinitely. Jet cannot promise zero telemetry while leaving those facts implicit.

The safe mental model is two doors. `jet report` opens the local door and never reaches the network. A later sharing step opens the network door only after the person inspects the bundle and names or accepts its destination. This ballot chooses whether Jet owns that second door.
decisions.story: Amara maintains a hospital service on a restricted workstation. A Jet compiler problem appears, so she creates and reads a local report. Before sharing it, she must know the receiver, the account used, the server facts exposed, and when the copy will be deleted.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet report
wrote local report bundle to .jet/reports/8c9d…
$ less .jet/reports/8c9d…/README.txt
$ less .jet/reports/8c9d…/report.txt

# What, if anything, should the next explicit step do?
$ jet report --send .jet/reports/8c9d…

options.name: Keep sharing outside Jet
options.detail: Jet creates and explains the local bundle, then stops. The person attaches it through a support channel they already trust. Jet never handles a destination, account credential, or network request.
options.technical: Do not ship `jet report --send`. Amend the illustrative D-TELEMETRY1 example so its separate explicit sharing step is manual. Jet's privacy boundary ends at the local content-hash directory.
options.code:
$ jet report
wrote local report bundle to .jet/reports/8c9d…
$ less .jet/reports/8c9d…/report.txt
# Attach the directory to the chosen private issue or support case.

options.name: Send to a fixed Jet report inbox
options.detail: Jet sends only to one project-owned service. No account is required. The service sees the source address and request time, keeps the bundle for 30 days, then deletes it.
options.technical: `jet report --send <bundle>` performs one HTTPS POST to `https://reports.jet-lang.org/v1/bundles` using system certificate roots. It sends the two bundle files and their content hash. No cookies or stable client identifier are sent. The server returns an opaque receipt. Server access logs and bundle data have a 30-day maximum retention.
options.code:
$ jet report --send .jet/reports/8c9d…
destination: https://reports.jet-lang.org/v1/bundles
includes: README.txt, report.txt
server observes: source address and request time
retention: at most 30 days
sent; receipt: R-4M7K2

options.name: Attach to a named GitHub issue
options.detail: The person names a Jet issue. Jet uses an existing GitHub login, so GitHub and the issue readers learn the account identity. Retention and visibility follow that issue.
options.technical: `jet report --send <bundle> --issue <Jet GitHub issue URL>` invokes the installed `gh` client. `gh` owns HTTPS transport and OAuth credentials; Jet never reads the token. Only issues in the configured Jet organization are accepted. Public issues make the bundle public and retain it with issue history; private issue access follows repository policy.
options.code:
$ jet report --send .jet/reports/8c9d… \
    --issue https://github.com/jet-lang/jet/issues/412
destination: public GitHub issue #412
identity: existing gh login
retention: issue history
attach these two files? [y/N]

options.name: Send to a destination named each time
options.detail: Experts can name any secure web endpoint. This gives organizations full control, but Jet cannot promise who receives the data or how long that receiver keeps it.
options.technical: `jet report --send <bundle> --to <https-url>` performs one HTTPS POST with the two files and content hash. Optional authentication comes only from `--token-env <NAME>`; Jet reads that named value and sends it as a bearer token. Redirects, plain HTTP, local addresses, and credentials embedded in URLs are rejected. Destination privacy and retention belong to the named receiver.
options.code:
$ jet report --send .jet/reports/8c9d… \
    --to https://support.example.org/jet \
    --token-env ACME_SUPPORT_TOKEN
destination: support.example.org
receiver controls identity and retention
send these two files? [y/N]

comparisons.note: Rust bug reports commonly use local verbose version output that the person pastes into an issue. The compiler does not own a general report-upload service.
comparisons.code:
$ rustc --version --verbose
# Inspect, then paste into the chosen issue.

comparisons.note: Go telemetry separates local collection from upload and uses an explicit opt-in plus a fixed project service. That is closest to a project-owned version of option B.
comparisons.code:
$ go telemetry local
$ go telemetry on

comparisons.note: Browsers often show a send choice after a crash. The vendor owns the fixed destination, privacy notice, and retention contract.
comparisons.code: Send crash report to the browser vendor? [ ]

recommendation.why: Manual sharing preserves the permanent zero-telemetry promise without making Jet a data receiver. The person keeps destination, identity, visibility, and retention inside a support channel they already chose.

whyNot.reason: A Jet inbox creates a new store of user data, an exposed service, and a retention promise before the project has an operating owner for any of them.
GitHub identity and issue visibility become part of a supposedly simple compiler command, and public issue history can preserve a report indefinitely.
An arbitrary receiver prevents Jet from stating one useful privacy or retention promise and makes a mistaken destination a direct disclosure.

recommendation.tradeoff: The person must attach two small text files manually. That extra step is acceptable because it keeps every network transfer visible and owned by the chosen support channel.

decisions.title: Optional narrowing after presence checks
decisions.gist: Choose when an Optional check lets later code use its payload directly.
decisions.lesson:
An optional value has either a payload, written `Val(value)`, or no payload, written `None`. Code must prove a payload exists before using it as the inner type.

Flow narrowing lets the compiler remember a Boolean check. After `if user != None`, the compiler may treat stable `user: User?` as `User` only where that check proves it is present.

A stable name cannot change while the proof is used. An immutable local or parameter is stable. Mutable storage, fields, indexes, aliases, and fresh calls may change or be evaluated again.

A binding pattern proves the same fact while creating a payload name. `if user == Val(found)` makes `found: User` available inside the branch. Jet already ratifies and ships this pattern form.

This choice controls how much the compiler remembers automatically, which style documentation teaches, and where programmers must bind the payload explicitly. Every option stays memory-safe and keeps the existing runtime representation.
decisions.story: Maya handles an optional signed-in customer in a checkout service. She checks for `None`, then wants to read the customer email without a fallback, cast, or repeated pattern ceremony.

options.name: Flow-first for stable names
options.detail: A `None` check narrows an immutable local or parameter. Patterns remain the explicit tool for computed values, mutable storage, fields, or a new payload name.
options.technical: For direct immutable identifiers of type `T?`, `x != None` narrows `x` to `T` in the true branch. `x == None` narrows `x` to `T` in the false branch. The fact reaches the right side of short-circuit `&&`, but not `||`, and ends at the branch boundary. Mutable locals, field paths, indexes, aliases, and calls never narrow. `x == Val(v)` keeps its existing binding behavior. Sema records a proven unwrap in typed IR; codegen performs no proof or speculative check. Documentation teaches the `None` check for a direct stable name and the binding pattern for every other case.

options.name: Binding patterns only
options.detail: A `None` check never changes a type. Programmers always bind the payload with the existing pattern before using it.
options.technical: Keep current semantics. `x == None` and `x != None` produce `Bool` only. `if x == Val(v)` proves presence and introduces `v: T` in the true branch and short-circuit `&&` tail. Computed expressions and places use the same pattern engine. No implicit unwrap enters typed IR.

options.name: Flow narrowing and patterns everywhere safe
options.detail: Both styles are normal. Flow analysis also follows immutable field paths, while patterns remain available for binding and destructuring.
options.technical: Apply Option facts to immutable identifiers and deeply immutable field paths. Invalidate a fact on any write to its root, mutable borrow, escaping alias, or call that may reach that root. Carry facts through `&&`, branch complements, early exits, and nested control flow. Keep all S31 pattern bindings as equal canonical style. Sema must encode each proven unwrap in typed IR so codegen stays mechanical.

comparisons.note: Kotlin smart-casts after a null check when the compiler can prove the value cannot change.
Swift normally unwraps by binding a new non-optional name. A plain nil comparison does not change the original type.
Rust uses pattern binding for `Option`; a comparison does not turn the original value into its payload.
comparisons.code: if let Some(user) = user { println!("{}", user.name); }

comparisons.note: TypeScript tracks checks through control flow and narrows many expressions, then widens them when assignments can invalidate the fact.

recommendation.why: A makes the obvious direct check useful for beginners while limiting hidden proof state to names that cannot change. Existing patterns still handle payload naming and unstable expressions explicitly.

whyNot.reason: B preserves one explicit idiom, but forces a second name after an already conclusive presence check. That ceremony burdens the common beginner path.
C makes field access depend on invisible invalidation rules around writes, aliases, and calls. Users may struggle to predict when a previously valid read widens again.

recommendation.tradeoff: A does not narrow fields or mutable locals, even when a person can see they stay unchanged. Bind the payload explicitly in those cases.

decisions.title: What happens when a reactive value crosses into another task?
decisions.gist: Choose what Jet does when a live reactive value, such as a Signal, is handed to another task. Stop it at compile time, watch it at run time, or make it work safely.
decisions.lesson:
A reactive value is a box that holds data and tells its watchers when the data changes. In Jet these boxes are `Signal<T>`, `Derived<T>`, and `Computed<T>`. An `Effect` is a watcher that runs when they change. A dashboard can watch a `Signal<Int>` and redraw each time the number changes.

A task is a piece of work that can run on another processor core at the same time as your main code. Two tasks can touch the same memory at the same moment. When at least one of them writes, and nothing orders the two touches, the result is a data race. A race can corrupt data or change behavior from run to run.

Jet checks every value that crosses into a task or a channel. This check is called sendability. Plain owned data may cross. `Shared<T>` may cross because its lock orders every read and write. Today's reactive boxes are built for one thread only, so they must not cross.

Here is the bug this ballot closes. Sema lets a reactive box cross into a task. The hidden Rust compiler then rejects the generated code, and the build dies with an internal compiler error (exit 101). That breaks the rule that sema owns every user-facing check. This ballot picks the lawful behavior at the boundary.
decisions.story: Priya builds a live order dashboard. She captures a `Signal<Int>` in a background refresh task. The compiler accepts her code, then the native build dies with an internal compiler error. She never learns what she did wrong or what to type instead.

options.name: Stop the crossing at compile time
options.detail: Reactive boxes stay inside the task that made them. A task capture, a channel send, a task result, or a parallel callback that moves one across is a compile error. The error teaches the fix: send owned copies through a channel, or hold plain shared state in `Shared<T>`. Workers never touch a live reactive graph.
options.technical: Add an explicit thread-boundary status for every compiler-known Core handle. Mark `Signal<T>`, `Derived<T>`, `Computed<T>`, and `Effect` thread-confined. Reuse the existing recursive sendability walk so lists, tuples, options, results, structs, enums, `Shared<Signal<T>>`, task results, and channel elements inherit the leaf failure. `tasks.spawn`, `g.task`, task results, and `Sender.send` emit E1102. The four `para_*` adapters emit E1111. Remove the reactive-handle capture exemption that currently clones `Rc` into worker closures. Add exact UI snapshots for direct and nested Signal, Derived, and Computed crossings through tasks, task groups, channels, and parallel adapters. Add AOT and dev/JIT parity tests that prove sema stops every case before codegen or rustc. Audit every opaque Core handle against its emitted Rust representation; no compiler-known handle defaults to sendable without a recorded status.

options.name: Allow the crossing; watch for races while the program runs
options.detail: Reactive boxes may move between tasks. The whole reactive runtime changes to thread-safe storage with an always-on conflict detector. Two clashing accesses stop the program with a Jet-owned runtime error. Code can share live reactive graphs, but a race only shows when a bad timing path actually runs. A program can pass every test and still stop in production.
options.technical: Replace the complete reactive graph's `Rc`, `Weak`, `RefCell`, `Cell`, thread-local observer stacks, and `Rc<dyn Fn()>` callbacks with thread-safe ownership and synchronization. Record task identity and access mode at each Signal, Derived, Computed, and Effect operation. Detect overlapping writes or read/write conflicts before the payload access and return one registered E3xxx runtime diagnostic with UI snapshot and `jet explain` coverage. Define deterministic ordering for subscriber delivery, derived recomputation, unsubscribe, drop, cancellation, and nested effects across tasks. Apply the same representation in AOT and dev/JIT. Add adversarial stress tests for task, task-group, channel, and parallel crossings, including nested handles, cancellation, and concurrent recomputation.

options.name: One Signal type; the compiler upgrades a box that crosses
options.detail:
Every reactive box starts in the fast one-thread form. When sema sees a box cross into a task, it rebuilds that one box in a lock-guarded thread-safe form. The crossing becomes legal, and no race is possible, at compile time. Code that never crosses pays nothing.

Beginners get working code with no new words and no runtime failure mode. Experts can pin a box with `#Local` to forbid the upgrade, or `#Shared` to force it. `jet report` lists every upgraded box, so the cost is auditable.
options.technical: The sendability walk marks each reactive allocation site whose handle reaches a task, task-group, channel, task-result, or parallel boundary, including handles nested inside other values. Marked sites lower to a synchronized representation (atomic refcount plus lock) with the same public API; unmarked sites keep `Rc`/`RefCell`. Define one deterministic law for cross-task subscriber delivery, derived recomputation, unsubscribe, drop, cancellation, and nested effects; where both forms apply it must match the single-thread order. `#Local` pins the fast form and turns a crossing into E1102; `#Shared` pins the synchronized form; both names ship through the syntax registry (I7). AOT and dev/JIT share the lowering. Snapshot the upgrade report. No runtime detector exists; every access is lock-ordered, so a data race cannot compile.

options.name: Two named forms; the writer picks local or shared
options.detail: Keep today's fast `Signal<T>` one-thread only; a crossing is a compile error, as in option A. Add a second family, `reactive.shared_signal`, that is lock-guarded and may cross tasks freely. The writer picks the form up front, and the source always shows which form is in play. The cost: a beginner must learn two names for one idea, and the compile error becomes a normal step on the path to a working program.
options.technical: Same synchronized reactive runtime as option C, exposed as distinct public types (`SharedSignal<T>`, `SharedComputed<T>`) instead of an inferred representation. The local family is thread-confined exactly as in option A (E1102/E1111, same snapshots), with a fix-it that names the shared family. No inference; no representation change behind the source. Names ship through the syntax registry (I7).

comparisons.note: Rust checks `Send` and `Sync` before a value enters a thread. `Rc<RefCell<T>>` is rejected; `Arc<RwLock<T>>` is the explicit shared form. This is option D: two named forms, the writer picks.
comparisons.code:
std::thread::spawn(move || signal.set(1));
// error: Rc<RefCell<_>> cannot be sent between threads safely

comparisons.note: Swift strict concurrency checks `Sendable` at task boundaries and rejects unprotected reference state. Static rejection, like options A and D. No compiler upgrades a value's form for you.
comparisons.code:
Task.detached { model.update() }
// error: task-isolated value passed as a strongly transferred parameter

comparisons.note: Go permits shared memory and offers a race detector only in selected test or run builds. Programs ship without it. Option B is this idea made always-on.
Signals never cross a worker boundary; workers only receive message copies. This is option A's world, enforced by the platform rather than a compiler.
comparisons.code: worker.postMessage(snapshot) // copies data; no live signal crosses

recommendation.why: Option C is the only option where every program is race-free at compile time and the beginner's first background task still just works. Sema owns the whole decision, rustc stays hidden, and the surface stays one mechanism: one Signal with one meaning everywhere. The pins and the upgrade report give experts exact control and a full audit.

whyNot.reason: The beginner's most natural program becomes a compile error, and the cure is channel plumbing they have not learned yet.
A race survives compilation and only shows when a bad timing path runs; tests can pass and production can stop.
It makes every writer pick a representation up front and makes a beginner learn two names for one idea.

recommendation.tradeoff: A box's runtime cost can change because a distant task captures it, with no edit at the box itself. The `#Local` pin and the upgrade report exist to expose and control exactly that.

decisions.title: Exact XML typed projection and helper surface
decisions.gist: Choose how typed XML decoding and common tree navigation appear in Jet code.
decisions.lesson:
An XML parser produces an ordered tree. That tree preserves details such as prefixes, namespace declarations, comments, CDATA sections, entity references, and original token spelling.

Application structs usually need a simpler view. A typed projection maps the root element into Codable fields. Attributes use names beginning with @. Child elements use expanded names. Simple text uses $text. Mixed content uses $content without reordering it.

An expanded name identifies an XML name by namespace address and local name. The compact spelling is called a Clark name. For example, {urn:shop}price means local name price in namespace urn:shop. Prefixes such as s:price are document aliases, not stable identities.

The ratified XML law already fixes the tree, security rules, projection keys, mixed-content behavior, and error type. It also requires xml.decode<T>. This decision does not reopen those rules.

The open choice is the helper view. A helper may return a small typed value, the original DataTree node, or a Clark string. All three can describe the same XML name. They differ in ceremony and retained detail.

Typed decoding first parses one complete document. It then projects the single root element. Parse failures keep source locations. Projection failures use XMLError kind Shape, no source location, and the deepest known projected path.

A simple element can decode directly into a scalar target from $text. A struct target sees attributes, child keys, $text, and $content. Repeated children become arrays. Existing Rename and DenyUnknownFields rules still apply.
decisions.story: Mina imports supplier catalogs. Most fields map cleanly into structs, but prices use namespaces and attributes. She also inspects comments and mixed descriptions when a supplier sends an unusual document.

options.name: Focused helpers with a typed name view
options.detail: Ship symmetric text and byte typed decoding. The four focused helpers cover the common navigation path. expanded_name returns a named tuple with every name component. Beginners get .local, while experts retain prefix and namespace evidence.
options.technical: Signatures are decode<T: Codable>(text: String, options: XMLParseOptions = XMLParseOptions.safe()) -> T ? XMLError; decode_bytes<T: Codable>(bytes: [U8], options: XMLParseOptions = XMLParseOptions.safe()) -> T ? XMLError; root(document: DataTree) -> DataTree ? XMLError; expanded_name(node: DataTree) -> (raw: String, prefix: String?, local: String, namespace_uri: String?) ? XMLError; attribute(element: DataTree, name: String) -> String? ? XMLError; content(element: DataTree) -> [DataTree] ? XMLError. attribute selectors are local names or Clark names, never prefixes. It returns normalized_value. A found attribute with an unresolved entity returns Entity. content returns exact child nodes in source order. No additional query or wrapper type ships.
options.code:
document := xml.parse(source)?
root := xml.root(document)?
name := xml.expanded_name(root)?
print(name.local)
print(name.namespace_uri ?? "none")
print(xml.attribute(root, "{urn:shop}id")? ?? "missing")
for child in xml.content(root)? {
    print(xml.expanded_name(child)?.local)
}

catalog := xml.decode<Catalog>(source)?
copy := xml.decode_bytes<Catalog>(wire)?

options.name: Tree-native helpers
options.detail: Keep every helper result inside ordinary DataTree. This exposes all lexical and entity evidence without another view shape. Routine navigation needs more field access and validation code.
options.technical: decode and decode_bytes match option A. root(document) returns the root DataTree. expanded_name(node) returns the exact XMLName DataTree object. attribute(element, name) returns the exact attribute DataTree node or None. content(element) returns exact child nodes. Selectors use local or Clark names. Helper shape failures return XMLError Shape. No typed XMLName or generic query surface ships.
options.code:
document := xml.parse(source)?
root := xml.root(document)?
name := xml.expanded_name(root)?
print((name.field("local")? ?? DataTree.Text("missing")).text()? )

price := xml.attribute(root, "{urn:shop}price")?
if price != None {
    node := price ?? panic("checked")
    print(node.field("normalized_value")?)
}

catalog := xml.decode<Catalog>(source)?
copy := xml.decode_bytes<Catalog>(wire)?

options.name: Clark-string helpers
options.detail: Return namespace-stable Clark strings and normalized attribute text. This keeps the helper surface compact. Code that needs original prefixes or raw name spelling must inspect the underlying tree.
options.technical: decode and decode_bytes match option A. root(document) returns DataTree. expanded_name(node) returns String using local for no namespace and {namespace_uri}local otherwise. attribute(element, name) returns normalized String or None. content(element) returns exact child nodes. Selectors use the same Clark grammar. No XMLName view or generic query surface ships.

comparisons.note: C# separates stable expanded names from document prefixes. XName carries namespace and local name, while XElement preserves the tree.
comparisons.code:
XName name = XName.Get("price", "urn:shop");
string? currency = element.Attribute("currency")?.Value;

comparisons.note: Java maps attributes and text into annotated fields. Tree navigation remains a separate API for mixed or unusual documents.
Rust commonly uses @field for attributes and $text for element text. Namespace-sensitive navigation still needs explicit expanded-name handling.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Price {
    #[serde(rename = "@currency")]
    currency: String,
    #[serde(rename = "$text")]
    amount: String,
}

recommendation.why: Option A matches the ratified beginner example and keeps namespace identity visible without forcing raw DataTree field access. Four helpers remain a small view over one canonical tree.

whyNot.reason: Tree-native results preserve everything, but they make common name and attribute reads repeat schema checks that the format adapter already knows.
Clark strings are excellent selectors, but returning only a string hides prefix and raw-name evidence during ordinary namespace debugging.

recommendation.tradeoff: The expanded-name tuple briefly duplicates four fields already stored in DataTree. It is an immutable view, not a second document model or serialization mechanism.

decisions.title: Typed data streaming and invalid-data policy
decisions.gist: Choose how large typed data stays bounded and how invalid analysis results are represented.
decisions.lesson:
Whole-value data calls read everything before returning. A streaming reader returns one typed row when the caller asks. That pull model creates backpressure because no hidden producer queue can grow.

A memory bound limits storage owned by the operation. Parsing needs a wire buffer and one decoded item. Sorting, joining, grouping, and collecting retain more state, so each needs an explicit ceiling.

Clean end-of-input is not an error. A reader returns None only after validating the complete input. Malformed bytes, a bad row, an I/O failure, or a crossed limit returns a typed error value.

Partial I/O may happen after earlier rows were returned. Those complete rows stay valid. The unfinished row never escapes, terminal errors repeat unchanged, and a failed collect returns no partial table.

Some numeric operations have no honest ordinary result. Examples include the mean of no values, a quantile outside zero through one, a zero-width window, and statistics containing NaN or infinity.

Signed zero also needs a rule because positive and negative zero compare equal but can print differently. Pivot keys need separate row and column identity because joining strings with a delimiter can collide.

Jet already has bounded pull readers, EncodingLimits, and EncodingError in core.encoding. The data layer should reuse that parser and ownership law, then add typed row and analysis meaning.
decisions.story: Maya processes a 90 GB event export on a small build worker. She needs bounded grouping, cancellation during a blocked read, and an exact error instead of a plausible zero.
decisions.inWild:
use core.data as data
use core.encoding as encoding
use core.files as files

#[Codable]
struct Event {
    service: String
    latency_ms: Float
}

input :: files.open("events.csv") ?? panic("open")
limits := data.DataLimits.safe()
limits.encoding.max_total_bytes = Val(100_000_000_000)
reader :: data.csv_reader<Event>(^input, limits) ?? panic("reader")
summary :: data.group_mean(reader, e => e.service, e => e.latency_ms)
if summary == {
    Ok(groups) -> print(data.bar_text(groups) ?? panic("plot"))
    Err(error) -> print("{error.kind}: {error.reason}")
}

options.name: One fallible typed pull pipeline
options.detail: Streaming, decoding, limits, and invalid analytics use one DataError. Undefined or invalid results never become plausible numbers. Existing operation names also accept the typed stream.
options.technical:
Add opaque DataStream<T>, csv_reader<T>, and json_reader<T>. Constructors consume FileReader and reuse the matching core.encoding reader without another parser.

DataStream.next returns T? ? DataError. DataStream is not Codable, Copy, or Clone. Clean EOF is stable None after complete validation.

DataLimits contains encoding: EncodingLimits, max_groups: Int, max_sort_rows: Int, max_join_rows: Int, and max_output_rows: Int. safe uses EncodingLimits.safe(), 100000, 1000000, 1000000, and 1000000.

Invalid limits fail before I/O. A crossing fails before retaining the item that crosses it. Filter and scalar reducers remain streaming; sort, join, pivot, group, and collect enforce their named bound.

Synchronous next provides backpressure. Cancellation follows D-CANCELMODEL1 at the underlying read wait point, unwinds the task, and drops the handle. It is not mislabeled as decoding failure.

DataErrorKind is Decode, Limit, IO, Empty, InvalidArgument, NonFinite, Overflow, or State. DataError stores kind, operation, row, column, index, reason, and an optional handle-free EncodingError cause.

DataError derives Clone and Eq. Encoding failures project location and cause without loss. The first terminal error is latched and every later read returns an equal clone.

sum of empty data is 0.0. Mean, min, max, median, variance, standard deviation, and describe return Empty on empty data.

Quantile requires a finite q in 0.0 through 1.0 and uses linear interpolation. Rolling width must be positive. Neither argument is clamped.

Every numeric reducer rejects the first non-finite input by index. Finite overflow returns Overflow. Sum uses deterministic Neumaier compensation; population variance uses deterministic Welford order.

Computed zero outputs normalize to positive zero, while raw Series values preserve their sign. Plots reject negative counts and non-finite values.

Replace pivot string keys with DataPivotCell fields row_key, column_key, count, sum, and mean. Distinct key pairs can never collide.

Edition 2027 changes affected functions to return DataError and changes pivot_sum to DataPivotCell. Jet fix inserts propagation or an explicit panic and flags pivot field uses for review.

Edition 2026 keeps its existing signatures and bytes frozen. New streaming and corrected analysis behavior belong only to the current edition, so one current mechanism remains.

options.name: Nullable statistics with layered errors
options.detail: Empty statistics return None, while invalid arguments and stream failures use separate error families. Callers retain precise layers, but composed pipelines handle nested absence and failure.
options.technical:
Typed pull readers and DataLimits match option A. Wire and I/O failures remain EncodingError, row projection returns DecodeError, and numeric failures use DataMathError.

A reader item is Result<T, DecodeError> inside the fallible encoding stream. Mean, min, max, median, variance, standard deviation, and describe return Float? or DataSummary?.

Quantile returns Float? ? DataMathError because empty input is None and invalid q is an error. Rolling mean returns [Float] ? DataMathError.

NaN and infinity remain ordinary Float values and propagate through reducers. Computed signed zero is preserved. Plots reject non-finite or negative geometry with DataMathError.

Pivot returns DataPivotCell with separate keys. Stream cancellation and partial-I/O law match option A. Every materializing operation still enforces DataLimits.

This option also needs an edition transition for nullable returns and pivot cells. It does not unify error handling across one pipeline.
options.code:
reader :: data.csv_reader<Event>(^input, limits)?
next :: reader.next()?                 // Result<Event, DecodeError>?

mean :: data.mean(latencies)           // Float?
p95 :: data.quantile(latencies, 0.95)? // Float?
print(mean ?? "no rows")

// A NaN remains a Float and can reach later calculations.
print(data.mean([0.0 / 0.0]))

options.name: Keep compatibility through checked twins
options.detail: Current functions keep their sentinel and clamping behavior. New checked names provide bounded streams and typed failures. Old code stays source-compatible, but Jet carries two analysis meanings.
options.technical:
Add csv_reader, json_reader, DataStream, DataLimits, and DataError with the streaming law from option A. Existing eager statistics and pivot_sum remain unchanged.

Add try_mean, try_quantile, try_rolling_mean, try_pivot_sum, and matching checked names. Checked calls use option A numeric and pivot laws.

The old names keep empty 0.0 results, quantile clamping, width coercion, non-finite propagation, and delimiter-joined pivot keys. Documentation must teach which family is safe.

No edition migration is required. This option intentionally keeps parallel mechanisms and cannot make unqualified existing calls satisfy the stricter data-quality contract.
options.code:
legacy :: data.mean([])                 // 0.0
legacy_q :: data.quantile(values, 1.5)  // silently clamps to 1.0

checked :: data.try_mean(values)?
checked_q :: data.try_quantile(values, q)?
cells :: data.try_pivot_sum(rows, row_key, column_key, value)?

// Both families remain public.

comparisons.note: Jet already uses synchronous pull readers, explicit limits, stable EOF, latched terminal errors, and no hidden queue. Typed data can reuse that exact transport law.
SQL count has an empty identity, while most other aggregates return NULL on no rows. That distinguishes zero from missing information but does not explain invalid numeric input.
A pull iterator yields one item at a time. Fallible pipelines commonly carry Result items, making the failure position explicit without a background producer.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one failure shape and gives experts exact locations, limits, cancellation, numeric laws, and partial-I/O behavior. It also preserves one operation vocabulary.

whyNot.reason: B makes empty input visible, but nested optional and error results complicate composition. Non-finite values can still travel as apparently valid Float values.
C avoids migration, but every analysis has safe and legacy meanings. Unqualified existing calls remain capable of plausible wrong answers and pivot collisions.

recommendation.tradeoff: A requires an edition migration and explicit error handling at affected call sites. In exchange, current-edition code has one auditable meaning and no silent numeric coercion.

decisions.title: Built-in HTTP Handler wrappers: timeout, body limit, CORS, and compression
decisions.gist: Pick how Jet spells Handler wrappers for timeouts, body size limits, CORS, and compression.
decisions.lesson:
An HTTP Handler takes one request and returns one response. A Handler wrapper is a Handler that calls another Handler. The inner Handler does the real work. The outer Handler adds one policy, such as a time budget or a size cap.

Other stacks often call this middleware. That word can suggest a hidden framework layer or a next-callback chain. Jet already treats the server as plain Handler composition. So this ballot prefers words that say wrap and policy.

A request timeout cancels work when the budget runs out. A body limit rejects an oversized request body before the app keeps the whole payload. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) sets which other websites may call your API in a browser. Response compression shrinks bytes when the client can decode them.

D-HTTP-SERVER2 already showed recover and access_log as nested wrappers. Its examples used the path http.middleware. This ballot chooses the everyday public spelling for those wrappers and for the four new policies.
decisions.story: Maya ships a public JSON API. She wants a one-line body cap on uploads. She also needs a search timeout, CORS for her web app, and gzip for large JSON.
decisions.inWild:
app :: http.wrap.access_log(
  http.wrap.cors(.Allow.{ origins: ["https://app.example"], methods: ["GET", "POST"] },
    http.wrap.timeout(Duration.seconds(5)?,
      http.wrap.body_limit(1*MiB,
        http.wrap.compress(.Gzip,
          router)))))
server :: http.Server.bind("0.0.0.0:8080", app)?

options.name: Nested http.wrap.* wrappers
options.detail: Each policy is one function under http.wrap. You nest them at startup. The name says wrap, not middleware. This renames the D-HTTP-SERVER2 example path.
options.technical: Signatures stay Handler->Handler or (Policy, Handler)->Handler. timeout cancels via ambient Context/task cancellation. body_limit enforces before retention past the cap. cors uses a typed policy value. compress negotiates Content-Encoding with the native gzip engine from D-DEP-HTTP2. static_files(root) stays the separate constructor from D-HTTP-SERVER2. access_log and recover move to http.wrap.* to match.
options.code:
app :: http.wrap.timeout(Duration.seconds(5)?,
  http.wrap.body_limit(1*MiB, router))
server :: http.Server.bind("0.0.0.0:8080", app)?

options.name: Flat http.* wrapper functions
options.detail: No nest folder. You write http.timeout and http.body_limit on the http module. Fewer path parts. The http root gets more names.
options.technical: Same Handler->Handler shape as A. Lives beside Client, Server, Router. Higher name-collision risk on the http module surface.
options.code:
app :: http.timeout(Duration.seconds(5)?,
  http.body_limit(1*MiB, router))
server :: http.Server.bind("0.0.0.0:8080", app)?

options.name: Keep http.middleware.* spelling
options.detail: Same nested wrappers as A, but keep the word middleware from D-HTTP-SERVER2 examples. Familiar to Express users. Keeps the misleading label.
options.technical: Identical mechanics to A. Only the module path stays http.middleware.*.
options.code:
app :: http.middleware.timeout(Duration.seconds(5)?,
  http.middleware.body_limit(1*MiB, router))
server :: http.Server.bind("0.0.0.0:8080", app)?

options.name: Router builder methods
options.detail: Policies hang off the router as chained methods. Fewer nested parentheses. The router becomes the policy bag and can hide where a limit applies.
options.technical: router.timeout(...).body_limit(...).cors(...).compress(...) returns Router or Handler. Global vs per-route attachment needs extra methods.
options.code:
router.timeout(Duration.seconds(5)?)
  .body_limit(1*MiB)
  .cors(.Allow.{ origins: ["https://app.example"] })
server :: http.Server.bind("0.0.0.0:8080", router)?

options.name: Server option struct only
options.detail: All four policies live on Server.bind options. Simple for one global policy. Per-route limits and mixed CORS need a second mechanism.
options.technical: ServerOptions { timeout, body_limit, cors, compress }. Fights D-HTTP-SERVER2 Handler composition and the nested access_log example.
options.code:
server :: http.Server.bind("0.0.0.0:8080", router, .
  { timeout: Duration.seconds(5)?, body_limit: 1*MiB })?

options.name: Defer wrappers; keep transport limits only
options.detail: Ship no ordinary Handler wrappers yet. Keep only transport deadlines and the default framing cap. Beginners lose the batteries D-HTTPDEPTH1 promised.
options.technical: Documents Open/Partial for these four. Does not remove static_files(root). access_log and recover still need a public spelling from this or a follow-up rename.

comparisons.note: People wrap Handler values with nested functions. They rarely put a middleware module name on the call.
Express calls the same idea middleware and registers it with app.use in order.
Tower names the unit Layer. A Layer wraps a Service the way Jet wraps a Handler.

recommendation.why: Nested http.wrap keeps one Handler mechanism for global and per-route policy, matches the ratified composition shape, and drops the misleading middleware label.

whyNot.reason: Flat http.* names work, but they crowd the http root and hide that these values are wrappers.
Keeps a word that suggests a framework layer Jet does not have.
Router methods invent a second attachment style and blur per-route scope.
Server options cannot express mixed per-route limits without another mechanism.
Leaves the batteries-included server incomplete for the most common production policies.

recommendation.tradeoff: Nested calls are noisier than a builder chain, and renaming http.middleware from D-HTTP-SERVER2 examples is a small spelling break.

decisions.title: One compiler core: how JIT and AOT stay feature-identical
decisions.gist: Pick the compiler structure that makes every new feature work in jet run and jet build on the same day, from one implementation.
decisions.lesson:
A compiler has two halves. The front half reads your code, checks it, and builds an internal form of the program. Jet's internal form is called TIR. The back half takes TIR and actually runs it.

Jet has one front half but three back halves. AOT (ahead-of-time, jet build) turns TIR into Rust text and asks rustc to make a fast binary. The JIT (just-in-time, jet run) turns TIR into machine code in memory using a library called Cranelift. An interpreter walks the program directly, slower but simple.

Each back half is separate code. A feature must be written up to three times before it works everywhere. When the JIT copy is missing, jet run stops with error E2211 and tells the user to use jet build. 262 example programs hit that today.

There is a second, quieter problem. TIR was built by refactoring the Rust-text emitter, so it stores small pieces of ready-made Rust text inside itself. The AOT engine can paste that text. The JIT cannot use text; it needs structured data. So the JIT falls behind by construction, not by neglect.

Production language runtimes solved this with tiers. One cheap engine (an interpreter) defines what programs do. A fast engine (a JIT) compiles the parts it covers. When the fast engine cannot handle a piece, it hands that piece to the cheap engine. Users never see a gap; coverage only changes speed. The choice here is which structure Jet commits to.
decisions.story: Priya teaches a beginners' class with Jet. Her lesson uses a map literal. She tested it with jet build, and it worked. In class, every student types jet run, because that is the obvious command. All of them hit E2211 and a message about a compiler defect. The feature exists, checked and correct — just not in the engine they used. She switches the class back to Python that afternoon.

options.name: Semantic core + one interpreter + speed tiers
options.detail: Rewrite TIR into a small set of structured facts with no Rust text. Build one interpreter over it; that interpreter defines what programs do, and comptime and the REPL use it too. jet run compiles each function with Cranelift when covered, and runs it in the interpreter when not. jet build keeps emitting Rust for rustc-grade binaries. A new feature is one lowering change; every engine gets it the same day. Gap errors like E2211 disappear; missing JIT coverage only means that function runs slower for now.
options.technical: TIR core: typed places, typed literals, symbol ids; Rust rendering moves entirely into the emit layer. Interpreter and both emitters hold exhaustive wildcard-free matches over the core. Per-function deopt over the existing host-shim ABI. R12 restates as: one semantic core, N exhaustive consumers, interpreter is the reference semantics. tests/jit_gaps.txt becomes a perf ratchet.
options.code:
// day 0: feature lands in parser + sema + lowering
$ jet run lesson.jet     // works now (interpreter tier for new construct)
42
$ jet build lesson.jet   // works now (AOT consumes the same core)
$ jet run --trace-tiers lesson.jet
run: tier1(native) helper: tier0(interp: map-literal)  // weeks later: all tier1

options.name: Keep two engines; hand-write every gap (today's path)
options.detail: Keep the current structure and finish card #729: hand-write a Cranelift lowering for all 262 gapped programs. Then hold parity with a CI gate that blocks any feature until both engines support it. Nothing about the compiler's shape changes. Every future feature is still written at least twice, and the gate is the only thing stopping a new gap. E2211 stays, ideally never seen because the gate catches gaps before release.
options.technical: Current R12 mechanism: two exhaustive consumers over emission-shaped TIR; parity enforced by tests/dev.rs and the #727 differential corpus gate. Rust-text fields in TIR remain; the JIT keeps parsing or special-casing them.
options.code:
// day 0: feature lands in lowering + Rust emitter
$ jet build lesson.jet   // works
$ jet run lesson.jet     // blocked in CI until the Cranelift arm is also written
Error [E2211]: Jet JIT has a compiler gap for this checked program.

options.name: One native engine for both: Cranelift compiles the binaries too
options.detail: Delete the Rust emitter. The same Cranelift lowering that serves jet run also writes native object files for jet build. One engine, perfect parity by construction. The costs: release binaries lose rustc's optimizer and run measurably slower, and the readable generated-Rust audit trail disappears. The 41k-line Rust runtime template layer must become a linkable runtime, and bridging to Rust crates gets harder.
options.technical: cranelift-object backend for AOT; jet-rt becomes the sole runtime linked into binaries; the I1 unsafe-audit story moves from generated Rust source to object-level review.
options.code:
$ jet build service.jet        // Cranelift object files, no rustc
$ ./service                     // correct, but ~1.5-3x slower than rustc -O today
$ jet run service.jet           // same lowering, always in sync

options.name: jet run becomes cached fast AOT
options.detail: Delete the Cranelift JIT. jet run compiles the same emitted Rust as jet build, but unoptimized and cached, then runs the result. Parity is perfect forever because there is only one engine. The cost lands on the run loop: the first run of any changed file waits on rustc, seconds even for hello world, and live hot-swap of a resident program loses per-function granularity.
options.technical: rustc with opt-level=0, incremental, shared target dir, dylib swap for resident dev. The devserver's R5 executor already owns half this machinery.
options.code:
$ jet run lesson.jet     // first run after an edit
... compiling (3.8s) ...
42
$ jet run lesson.jet     // unchanged file, warm cache
42   (0.1s)

comparisons.note: One bytecode. The interpreter defines behavior; C1/C2 JIT tiers only add speed. A feature works everywhere the day the bytecode lowering lands.
comparisons.code: javac Foo.java && java Foo   // never 'this opcode only works in the compiler'

comparisons.note: Ignition interpreter is the reference; TurboFan compiles hot functions and deopts back to Ignition on anything it cannot keep native. Users never see coverage.
The opposite bet: one fast AOT compiler, no JIT and no interpreter. Parity is trivial, but every run pays a compile, which Go accepts by making compiles very fast.
comparisons.code: go run main.go   // ~200ms compile for small files

recommendation.why: Option A is the only structure where 'written once, works everywhere, the same day' is guaranteed by the compiler's shape instead of by discipline and gates. Beginners never meet a coverage wall. Experts keep rustc-grade binaries and gain per-function tier visibility. It also honors the 2026-07-21 one-core decree at the structural level, not just the test level.

whyNot.reason: Every future feature still needs two hand-written engine arms, so gaps stay possible forever; the 262-program backlog shows the gate arrives after the wall, not before it.
Release binaries give up rustc's optimizer and the generated-Rust audit trail, trading the expert product's two strongest guarantees for parity that option A gets anyway.
Every edited file pays a rustc wait before it runs, which surrenders the instant run loop that makes jet run viable against Python for beginners.

recommendation.tradeoff: A construct without native coverage runs at interpreter speed until the Cranelift tier catches up, and nothing forces that catch-up except the performance ratchet. This also amends ratified law: R12's 'exactly two consumers' becomes 'one semantic core, every engine an exhaustive consumer, the interpreter is the reference.'

decisions.title: What jet run shows when the fast tier lacks coverage
decisions.gist: Decide what a user sees when jet run cannot compile part of a program natively and runs that part in the interpreter instead.
decisions.lesson:
jet run executes a program through tiers. Tier 1 is Cranelift: it compiles a function to machine code, so it runs fast. Tier 0 is the interpreter: it walks the program directly, correct but slower. When tier 1 cannot handle a function yet, the runtime can hand that one function to tier 0 and keep going. That handoff is called a deopt.

Today there is no handoff. Ratified rule D-LENS-RUN1 says a coverage gap is a hard stop: jet run prints error E2211 and tells the user to run jet build instead. That rule was honest at the time. The only fallback available was AOT — a different engine with different coverage and timing — so falling back would have hidden real compiler defects.

The one-core rework (D-ONECORE1) changes the premise. The interpreter becomes the reference: it defines what every program does, and the fast tier must match it. Falling back to the reference is not hiding a defect; it is running the official semantics at a slower speed.

So the honesty question becomes a visibility question. Should the user be told when part of their program took the slow path? Beginners mostly should not care. Experts tuning a service, or an agent watching a perf budget, genuinely need to see which functions stayed on tier 0 and why. This ballot picks the default, and D-LENS-RUN1 stays law for everything it says about never falling back to AOT.
decisions.story: Marco is on day two of Jet. His weather script is checked and valid, and it worked in the class demo through jet build. He types jet run weather.jet and gets a red error naming a compiler defect, with instructions to use a different command and file a report. He does not know what a JIT is. He concludes Jet is broken.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet run examples/features/text/string_parse.jet
Error [E2211]: Jet JIT has a compiler gap for this checked program.
  --> string_parse.jet:2:4
 Why: jet run uses the JIT lens and does not hide a JIT compiler gap by running AOT.
 Fix: run `jet build <file>` and the binary for now, then report E2211 with the detail below.

// The program is correct. The wall is internal compiler scheduling.

options.name: Silent deopt, expert trace on request
options.detail: The program just runs. Functions the fast tier covers run native; the rest run in the interpreter; output is identical either way. Nothing is printed about tiers. Experts and agents who care ask for it: jet run --trace-tiers lists every function, its tier, and the named reason for any deopt. The gap list stays in the repo as a performance ratchet that may only shrink.
options.technical: E2211 retires from the diagnostic registry. Named gap reasons persist as internal trace strings and in tests/jit_gaps.txt (CI ratchet: additions need a named reason in the same diff). --trace-tiers prints function, tier, reason, and per-tier time.
options.code:
$ jet run weather.jet
Rain likely after 15:00

$ jet run --trace-tiers weather.jet
run        tier1 native
parse_row  tier0 interp (string-parse result status)
Rain likely after 15:00

options.name: Deopt with a one-line notice in jet dev only
options.detail: Same tiered execution as option A, but the resident dev loop prints one dim line naming the functions that took the slow path, once per session. Plain jet run stays silent. The idea is gentle awareness for people already in a development session, without teaching beginners an error-shaped reflex for something that is not an error.
options.technical: Notice renders once per resident session on the jet dev status line, not stderr of the program; NO_COLOR and --quiet suppress it. jet run behaves exactly as option A.
options.code:
$ jet dev weather.jet
[dev] 2 functions on interpreter tier (parse_row, fmt_time) — run --trace-tiers for detail
Rain likely after 15:00

options.name: Keep the wall: E2211 stays a hard error
options.detail: Keep D-LENS-RUN1 exactly as ratified. A coverage gap in jet run remains a loud stop naming a compiler defect, even though the interpreter could run the program correctly. The pressure to close gaps stays maximal, because every gap blocks a user. The cost also stays: valid programs fail on the beginner's default command for internal scheduling reasons.
options.technical: No product change. tests/jit_gaps.txt remains a feature gate; card #729 must reach zero before the wall stops firing.
options.code:
$ jet run weather.jet
Error [E2211]: Jet JIT has a compiler gap for this checked program.
 Fix: run `jet build <file>` and the binary for now.

comparisons.note: Deopts are silent by default; --trace-deopt exists for people tuning hot code.
Interpreter-vs-JIT scheduling is invisible; -XX:+PrintCompilation opts into the detail.
Falls back from JIT traces to the interpreter constantly and never mentions it; speed is the only observable.

recommendation.why: Silence is the correct beginner default: the program is valid, the output is correct, and there is no action a beginner could take. The trace flag gives experts and agents strictly better visibility than today's error, naming every deopt and its reason instead of only the first. The ratchet keeps real pressure on coverage without putting a wall in front of users.

whyNot.reason: A once-per-session notice is either ignored noise for beginners or too little for experts, who need the per-function trace anyway.
It fails valid programs on the default command for internal scheduling reasons, which is exactly the beginner-hostile wall the one-core directive orders removed.

recommendation.tradeoff: A program can quietly run slower than expected until coverage lands, and only people who know the trace flag will learn why. The performance ratchet, not user pain, becomes the sole forcing function for closing tier-1 gaps.

decisions.title: Universal typed-literal head: Type.{ body } for every type
decisions.gist: One construction spelling: any type may sit in front of a .{ } literal body.
decisions.lesson:
Today .{ } is the literal body for records only: Point.{ x: 1, y: 2 } names the type, and a bare .{ … } takes its type from the surrounding context. Every other kind of value states its type somewhere else. A byte list needs a typed binding. A sized number needs a conversion call. That scatter is the main reason type annotations pile up on bindings.

This decision makes Type.{ body } the one head for every type. The body is written in that type's own literal notation: elements for lists, entries for maps, one value for scalars. The body elaborates against the head exactly as if it were passed to a parameter of that type. It never converts; a mismatched body is the ordinary type error.

Two details ride along. [T].{} becomes the explicit empty collection, while bare [] keeps working wherever context already supplies the type. And a one-expression body doubles as a type assertion: Int.{ fetch_rows() } compiles only if the call already returns Int.
decisions.story: Mara is writing a packet parser. She wants packet :: [U8].{ 42, 0, 0, 0, 3 } to read as one thought: the value names its own element width and the binding stays bare. Today she must write the type on the binding, away from the value it describes.

options.name: Universal Type.{ body } head
options.detail: Every literal that needs a type states it once, at the head of the value. Records, scalars, collections, empties, and assertions all share the shape already known from Point.{ }. Braces never compute or convert; parentheses stay for real work like .new and .from_int.
options.technical: Sema route: Type.{ body } is D-DOTCTOR2 expected-type elaboration with the head as the expected type. Scalar literal bodies get comptime range checks in the E0135 family (D-RANGETYPE1 precedent). A non-literal body of a different type is the ordinary mismatch diagnostic teaching from_*. Amends S29/D-DOTCTOR1/2 and D-EMPTY; adds no new token. Nested list bodies may be bare .{ … } or plain [ … ] — both elaborate against the element type.

options.name: Bare paren constructors: U8(250), [U8](42, 0, 0)
options.detail: Extends the D-API-CTOR1 bare Type(…) idiom instead: the elements become call arguments. Slightly shorter for scalars, but construction splits into two shapes — braces for records, parentheses for everything else — and a call spelling that does no work.
options.code:
limit :: U8(250)
packet :: [U8](42, 0, 0, 0, 3)
out := [String]()
origin :: Point.{ x: 0.0, y: 0.0 }   // records keep braces — two shapes remain

options.name: Status quo: typed bindings carry the type
options.detail: No new literal head. The binding annotation keeps doing this job, so the type keeps appearing away from the value, and the typed binding forms must stay in the grammar to serve it.

comparisons.note: No numeric suffixes; literals elaborate against the expected type, and UInt8(250) names it inline when context is missing.
.{ … } is the anonymous literal that takes its type from context — the same headed/bare duality this option completes.

recommendation.why: One head shape covers records, scalars, collections, empties, and assertions, so the language keeps a single construction glyph and bindings never need to carry types.

whyNot.reason: It splits construction into braces for records and parentheses for everything else, and makes a no-work literal look like a function call.
It keeps the type on the binding, away from the value, and preserves the doubled-type lines measured across the corpus.

recommendation.tradeoff: .{ } bodies now span literals and one-expression assertions, so sema must keep one rule airtight: a body elaborates against the head and never converts.

decisions.title: Bare bindings: retire the typed binding forms
decisions.gist: A binding is always bare — the typed forms name: Type :: expr and name: Type := expr are removed.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has five binding shapes today: x :: v, x := v, their typed twins x: Type :: v and x: Type := v, and reassignment x = v. The typed twins exist mostly because some values cannot state their own type — empty lists, sized numbers, uninitialized buffers. Once Type.{ body } heads exist (D-DOTCTOR3), every value can. The twins are left with one job: repeating what the value already shows.

This decision deletes them. A binding is name :: value or name := value, and nothing else. The rule becomes: where a value exists, the type rides the value; where no value exists — function signatures and struct fields — the type follows the name.

The removal is an immediate clean break. The old forms become ordinary parse errors, with no special teaching text and no retirement window.
decisions.story: Mara reviews a diff full of emp: Employee := Employee.{ … } lines. Every line states the type twice. She wants one place to look, one form to write, and one sigil to grep.

options.name: Remove the typed forms — immediate clean break
options.detail: Two binder spellings, total. Searching :: or := finds every binding; there is no third form to remember or teach. The old spellings fail with an ordinary parse error — no legacy path, no lint to police drift.
options.technical: Amends S1: the binding grammar productions for name: Type :: expr and name: Type := expr are deleted from the parser, formatter, and editor grammars. Corpus migration is mechanical: annotations delete where the value self-types; otherwise the annotation's type becomes the value's head (D-DOTCTOR3).
options.code:
emp := Employee.{ level: 3, title: "Staff" }
cache := Lru<String, Int>.new(2)
count :: Int.{ fetch_rows() }     // the assertion moved onto the value

packet: [U8] :: [1, 2]            // ordinary parse error — no special case

options.name: Keep typed forms as optional documentation, add a redundancy lint
options.detail: The grammar keeps the typed twins for readers who like an inline type, and a lint flags annotations that repeat the value's head. Two ways to state one fact remain in the language, and the lint argues with style drift forever.
options.code:
emp: Employee := Employee.{ level: 3 }   // lint: annotation repeats the value's type
count: Int :: fetch_rows()               // allowed: documents a computed value

options.name: Status quo
options.detail: Nothing changes. The doubled-type lines stay legal and unflagged, and the corpus keeps growing them.
options.code:
emp: Employee := Employee.{ level: 3, title: "Staff" }
packet: [U8] :: [42, 0, 0, 0, 3]

comparisons.note: Short declarations never carry a type; x := f() relies on the value, and tooling answers 'what type is x'.
Keeps optional binding annotations — the counterpoint. Most code omits them and leans on inlay hints, so the grammar carries a form style guides then discourage.

recommendation.why: It ends the doubled-type problem at the grammar instead of policing it, and it completes the one-place-for-types law: values carry types, signatures carry types, bindings never do.

whyNot.reason: Optional annotations keep two spellings for one fact, and the lint fights style drift forever instead of ending it.
It leaves the measured redundancy in place and blocks the one clean rule the rest of this batch builds on.

recommendation.tradeoff: Computed values lose inline types unless the author writes an Int.{ … } assertion head; hover and inlay tooling carry the rest. About 206 corpus bindings rewrite mechanically.

decisions.title: uninit becomes a literal body: [U8#4096].{ uninit }
decisions.gist: The uninit spelling moves inside the value's literal body, so no binding form exists just for it.
decisions.lesson:
uninit skips zero-fill for a buffer the program will overwrite before reading. Sema proves the write-before-read on every path, so safety never depends on the spelling. Today the spelling is special: uninit may only appear as the right side of := on a binding that carries a type annotation. That makes it the last construct that forces an annotated binding.

With the typed binding forms retired (D-BIND-BARE1) and Type.{ body } universal (D-DOTCTOR3), the trigger moves inside the body: [U8#4096].{ uninit }. The type sits on the value like every other literal. The flow proof, its diagnostics, and the use core.mem gate stay exactly as they are — only the spelling moves, the same way D-UNINIT-SENTINEL1 itself moved the earlier marker.
decisions.story: Rowan fills a scratch buffer from a C decoder. He wants the buffer's type on the value, like every other literal in the file — not on a binding form that exists only to host this one keyword.
decisions.inWild:
use core.mem
bytes: [U8#128] := uninit          // today: the last annotation-forced binding
fixed :: mem.Fixed.over(&bytes)

options.name: Body sentinel: Type.{ uninit }
options.detail: The uninitialized state is written where the contents would be, inside the one literal shape. uninit stays a contextual keyword, legal only as a whole .{ } body; anywhere else it is the ordinary error.
options.technical: Amends D-UNINIT-SENTINEL1: trigger only. Flow analysis (E0420/E0423/E0424), POD-only rule, MaybeUninit lowering, and the use core.mem gate are unchanged. Parser: uninit is valid solely as the entire body of a Type.{ } head.
options.code:
use core.mem
bytes := [U8#128].{ uninit }
fixed :: mem.Fixed.over(&bytes)
n := Int.{ uninit }               // scalars too — same proof engine

options.name: Static member: Type.uninit
options.detail: A member-access spelling: [U8#128].uninit. Reads like an API surface, but no other literal state is a member, so construction grows a second head shape for one keyword.
options.code:
use core.mem
bytes := [U8#128].uninit

options.name: Status quo: name: Type := uninit
options.detail: Keeps the annotated-binding trigger. If the typed binding forms are removed, this spelling has no grammar left to live in, so choosing it means keeping one binding exception forever.
options.code:
use core.mem
bytes: [U8#128] := uninit

comparisons.note: undefined is a value-position sentinel, but it rides an annotated declaration — the exact shape this batch retires.

recommendation.why: It folds the last annotation-forced construct into the universal literal head, leaving the language with zero special binding rules.

whyNot.reason: It mints a member-shaped second spelling for literal state; braces are the shape channel everywhere else.
It depends on the retired typed-binding grammar and would remain the language's only exception.

recommendation.tradeoff: uninit becomes the one keyword legal inside a literal body, and the parser must reject it in every other position with the ordinary error.

decisions.title: Language tooling packs for jet env
decisions.gist: How a beginner turns on a full language toolchain in a Jet env.
decisions.lesson:
A language pack is a named preset that pulls the tools people expect for one language.

Think of it as a shopping list the tool fills for you. For Rust that list usually means the compiler, the package tool, the language server, and the formatter.

Without packs, you name every package yourself. That is precise, but beginners must know the whole list.

With packs, one short enable line fills the common tools. Experts still need a way to pin versions and add or remove tools.

The stakes are beginner speed versus expert control, and whether Jet grows a second way to declare packages.
decisions.story: Maya opens a Jet repo to write a small Rust service. She wants cargo and rust-analyzer in one step, like devenv languages.rust.enable, without pasting a twelve-package list.

options.name: Typed language packs on env
options.detail: Beginners enable a language with one typed field. Packs expand into ordinary packages. Experts can still list packages and pin versions. One mechanism underneath.
options.technical: Add languages: map on env modules. Each Lang record has enable, optional version/channel, and optional extra packages. Expansion is pure data into the existing package realize path. No second resolver.

options.name: Explicit packages only
options.detail: Keep today’s model. Docs and jet add helpers teach the lists. No languages field. Beginners paste or generate package lists.
options.technical: No new env syntax. Rely on packages: and overlays. Helpers may print suggested package sets but do not invent a pack type.

options.name: Packs as recipes only, no env field
options.detail: Ship recipe macros or jet add --lang rust that write packages: for you. No lasting languages: field in env modules.
options.technical: Scaffolding writes ordinary packages into env.jet. Re-running the helper can drift from hand edits unless merge rules are defined.
options.code:
$ jet env add-lang rust
# rewrites env.jet packages: [..., rustc, cargo, rust-analyzer, ...]

options.name: Packs plus mandatory explicit confirm
options.detail: languages.enable only prints the package set and refuses until the user pastes it. Maximum explicitness; high ceremony.
options.technical: Enable is a doctor/suggest step, not realize. Conflicts with beginner magic defaults.
options.code:
$ jet env
error: languages.rust.enable needs packages: [rustc, cargo, ...] — paste to confirm

comparisons.note: languages.rust.enable bundles toolchain and helpers with version/channel options.
Usually lists packages by hand in devShell.buildInputs.

recommendation.why: Packs give beginners one clear enable line while still expanding into the same package realize path experts already use.

whyNot.reason: Forces every beginner to memorize toolchain package sets that devenv already proved people want as one toggle.
Scaffold rewrite fights hand edits and hides the live declaration readers expect in env.jet.
Adds ceremony without removing the need for a pack definition, so beginners still stall.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must maintain pack definitions per language. That cost is accepted to keep the beginner path short without a second package system.

decisions.title: Workflow profiles for jet env
decisions.gist: Whether Jet envs get named workflow profiles beyond env.dev / env.test overlays.
decisions.lesson:
A workflow profile is a named slice of an environment you turn on for a job.

Example slices: backend databases, frontend node tooling, or CI-only browsers.

Jet already has role overlays such as env.dev and env.test. Those cover common intents.

Devenv also adds named profiles you combine with flags, and profiles that auto-apply from hostname or username.

Auto profiles save typing. They can also surprise someone on a shared machine if a hostname flips services on.

The choice is how much profile power Jet adds on top of today’s overlays.
decisions.story: Sam maintains a monorepo. On the laptop they want frontend tools. On the CI host they want browsers and stricter env vars. They do not want three separate repos.

options.name: Overlays only
options.detail: Keep env.dev / env.test / env.build. Compose with imports. No named profiles and no hostname or user auto-apply.
options.technical: No new profile syntax. Monorepo uses imports:find and workspace.jet. CI selects jet env test explicitly.
options.code:
$ jet env dev
$ jet env test

options.name: Named profiles with extends, manual only
options.detail: Add named profiles you pass on the CLI. Profiles can extend each other. No hostname or user auto-apply.
options.technical: profiles: on env modules; jet env --profile frontend. Merge law reuses module merge + priority. Auto host/user profiles omitted.
options.code: $ jet env --profile backend --profile testing

options.name: Named profiles plus hostname/user auto
options.detail: Everything in B, plus profiles that activate from hostname or username like devenv. Maximum convenience; more surprise risk.
options.technical: profiles.hostname / profiles.user auto-merge with documented priority. Must show what activated in jet env info.
options.code:
$ jet env
# also applied: hostname.ci-server, user.sam

options.name: Imports-only composition, no profile noun
options.detail: Teach folder imports as the only compose tool. Avoid the word profile to prevent clash with package profiles.
options.technical: Deepen imports for remote locked env modules. Package profiles (D-JPK-PROFILE*) stay a separate concept.
options.code:
imports: find("./frontend")
imports: find("./backend")

comparisons.note: profiles with extends, --profile flags, and hostname/user auto activation.
env role overlays and imports:find without named workflow profiles.

recommendation.why: Named manual profiles cover monorepo and CI slices without surprising auto activation from hostname or username.

whyNot.reason: Overlays alone force awkward env names for every cross-cutting slice a monorepo needs.
Hostname and user auto-apply can enable services without an explicit command, which is a trust hazard on shared machines.
Imports help structure folders but do not give a first-class switch for temporary slices like testing browsers.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must teach profile as a workflow idea beside package profiles. Clear CLI naming and docs must keep the two concepts apart.

decisions.title: Beginner Jet env vs expert flake-parts
decisions.gist: Whether experts can use flake-parts while beginners keep a simple Jet env default.
decisions.lesson:
flake-parts is a Nix toolkit for splitting a project into reusable flake modules.

People use it to assemble languages, services, and shells from small pieces instead of one big file.

Jet already aims for one easy default: typed env modules that just work.

The dual-facet rule says beginners get magic defaults, and experts get explicit control of the same outcomes.

So the question is not whether Jet copies flake-parts as the only UI. It is whether the expert facet may opt into flake-parts composition and interop beside that default.
decisions.story: Alex wants new teammates on jet env with no Nix module homework. Riley maintains a large monorepo already split with flake-parts and needs Jet to consume and extend that graph without a rewrite.

options.name: Dual-facet: Jet default + expert flake-parts
options.detail: Beginners use typed env.* only. Experts can consume and compose flake-parts flakes through an explicit expert path. Same lock and realize engine underneath.
options.technical: Default: env modules + imports:find. Expert: U16/#783 bridge understands flake-parts module flakes; optional emit/import of flake-parts-compatible shards. No beginner requirement to touch flake-parts. I8 preserved: one realize path, two entry surfaces.
options.code:
$ jet env
# beginner repo → env.dev

$ jet env
# flake-parts repo → bridge activates modules; jet env info notes flake-parts

options.name: Jet env only — no flake-parts
options.detail: Experts rewrite flake-parts setups into Jet modules. Bridge may read plain flakes but not flake-parts module composition as a supported expert product.
options.technical: Keep U16 best-effort flake translate. Document flake-parts as unsupported; users flatten manually.
options.code:
$ jet bridge flake
# L0204 / unsupported: flake-parts modules — flatten into env.*

options.name: flake-parts as primary UX
options.detail: Teach flake-parts first. Jet env becomes a thin skin over module flakes. Beginners must learn Nix module composition.
options.technical: Inverts beginner default. Conflicts with epoch-4 vision of typed env without a second language.
options.code:
$ jet env
# requires flake-parts modules even for hello-world

options.name: Emit-only flake-parts, no consume
options.detail: Jet can generate flake-parts shards for Nix neighbors, but cannot activate an existing flake-parts monorepo as a first-class expert path.
options.technical: One-way bridge. Riley's existing repo still needs a rewrite to be consumed.
options.code:
$ jet bridge flake --emit-parts
# writes modules/; cannot jet env an upstream flake-parts tree

comparisons.note: Simple devenv.nix default; flake-parts users often embed devenv as a module inside a larger flake.
Dual-facet: beginner magic defaults; expert explicit control of the same mechanism.
comparisons.code:
module env.dev { ... }  // default
// expert flake-parts via bridge/opt-in

recommendation.why: Keeps the easy Jet env path for beginners while giving experts a real flake-parts consume and compose path on the same lock and realize engine.

whyNot.reason: Forces experts to abandon working flake-parts monorepos even though the owner asked for that expert path.
Makes Nix module composition the default and burdens beginners.
Only helps Jet export outward; it does not load the expert repos people already have.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet must maintain flake-parts interop tests and docs. That cost is accepted so the expert facet is real, not a slogan.

decisions.comment: Jet has its own package/module system that should already support single file vs flake parts style devenvs -> ensure alignment with those existing paradigms

decisions.title: Script-start warm budget vs peers
decisions.gist: Pick the warm script-start budget Jet enforces in CI against Bash, Python, and Node.
decisions.lesson:
A script-start budget is a time limit for launching a short program.

Cold start means the first run after a change. Warm start means a later run of the same unchanged files.

Peers are the tools people already use for tiny agent tasks: Bash, Python, and Node. Jet wants to feel like those tools for short scripts.

We measure the same tasks on Jet and on each peer. We take a median so one slow sample does not dominate. We also record a high tail so rare stalls are visible.

The budget is the CI rule that fails the build when Jet’s warm start is too slow for that rule. The method lives in tests and fixtures today. This ballot picks the number and comparison rule.
decisions.story: Maya runs tiny Jet scripts from an agent loop all day. After a file is unchanged, she expects the next jet run to feel like bash true. She needs one clear CI rule so that speed does not quietly regress.
decisions.inWild:
# fixtures: tests/fixtures/script_speed/noop.jet
$ jet run noop.jet   # cold, stores tier-1 module
$ jet run noop.jet   # warm hit; measure median of 5
# peers: bash -c true | python -c pass | node -e ""
# CI fails when warm Jet median breaks the chosen rule

options.name: Warm no-op ≤ 50 ms absolute
options.detail: CI fails if warm Jet no-op median is at or above 50 milliseconds on the CI machine class. Simple number. Ignores how fast Bash is on that host.
options.technical: Gate tests/run_cache.rs script_start_budget_fixtures_and_peers; process-spawn median of 5 after one populate; machine metadata required in evidence log.
options.code:
assert!(warm_median_ms < 50);
// peers logged, not compared

options.name: Warm no-op ≤ 2× fastest peer
options.detail: CI fails if warm Jet no-op median is more than twice the fastest available peer median on that host. Tracks peer machines. Allows Jet to stay a little slower than Bash.
options.technical: Compare against min(bash, python, node) when present; skip missing peers; still require at least one peer sample.
options.code:
let peer = min(bash, python, node);
assert!(warm_median_ms <= 2 * peer);

options.name: Warm no-op ≤ 100 ms sanity only
options.detail: Keep today’s provisional gate: warm Jet no-op median under 100 milliseconds. Log peer numbers for humans. Do not fail CI on peer ratio yet.
options.technical: Matches current tests/run_cache.rs assert warm_median < 100; peer medians are eprintln evidence only.
options.code:
assert!(warm_median_ms < 100);
eprintln!("peers: bash={:?} python={:?} node={:?}", …);

options.name: Warm no-op ≤ slowest peer
options.detail: CI fails if warm Jet is slower than the slowest measured peer. Harder than B when Node is slow; fails when Jet loses to every peer.
